papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and flexible approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable ones. When combined with careful choices—such as pre-training compact students, data-free distillation for privacy, adaptive multi-teacher strategies, feature-level imitation, and teacher-side learning—KD can deliver strong task performance with much smaller inference cost. However, KD is not a panacea: optimization gaps between teacher and student, propagation of teacher biases, and dataset mismatches can limit gains unless explicitly addressed. A pragmatic KD pipeline therefore integrates algorithmic innovations and fairness/optimization checks to realize both efficiency and reliable behavior in production NLP and deep learning systems.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer via Adversarial Belief Matching
papers_seen.abstract: Performing knowledge transfer from a large teacher network to a smaller student is a popular task in modern deep learning applications. However, due to growing dataset sizes and stricter privacy regulations, it is increasingly common not to have access to the data that was used to train the teacher. We propose a novel method which trains a student to match the predictions of its teacher without using any data or metadata. We achieve this by training an adversarial generator to search for images on which the student poorly matches the teacher, and then using them to train the student. Our resulting student closely approximates its teacher for simple datasets like SVHN, and on CIFAR10 we improve on the state-of-the-art for few-shot distillation (with 100 images per class), despite using no data. Finally, we also propose a metric to quantify the degree of belief matching between teacher and student in the vicinity of decision boundaries, and observe a significantly higher match between our zero-shot student and the teacher, than between a student distilled with real data and the teacher. Code available at: https://github.com/polo5/ZeroShotKnowledgeTransfer

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Explaining Knowledge Distillation by Quantifying the Knowledge
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a method to interpret the success of knowledge distillation by quantifying and analyzing task-relevant and task-irrelevant visual concepts that are encoded in intermediate layers of a deep neural network (DNN). More specifically, three hypotheses are proposed as follows. 1. Knowledge distillation makes the DNN learn more visual concepts than learning from raw data. 2. Knowledge distillation ensures that the DNN is prone to learning various visual concepts simultaneously. Whereas, in the scenario of learning from raw data, the DNN learns visual concepts sequentially. 3. Knowledge distillation yields more stable optimization directions than learning from raw data. Accordingly, we design three types of mathematical metrics to evaluate feature representations of the DNN. In experiments, we diagnosed various DNNs, and above hypotheses were verified.

papers_seen.author: Mcmillan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression for NLP: Strengths, Limits, and a Recipe for Deployment
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is the most practical and widely adopted strategy for compressing large NLP models into smaller, deployable students. When applied thoughtfully—matching soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, using task-aware layer mapping, and addressing data or privacy constraints—KD recovers most of a teacher’s performance while enabling large reductions in storage, latency, and power. However, effective deployment requires recognizing and mitigating limits such as capacity mismatch, distributional heterogeneity, and the risk of transferring teacher biases.

papers_seen.author: Higgins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller ones that meet deployment constraints. KD reduces storage, latency, and energy while preserving much of teacher performance, but its success depends on what knowledge is transferred, how teacher signals are generated and trusted, and how distillation is combined with other compression methods and fairness or robustness constraints. Effective deployment requires task-aware decisions about targets (logits vs. features), data (original, augmented, or synthetic), architectural alignment, and additional safeguards for bias and domain shift.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Cornerstone for Compressing Deep Models in NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic and broadly applicable strategy for compressing large deep models so they can be deployed under real-world constraints. By transferring predictive behavior or intermediate representations from a high-capacity teacher to a smaller student, KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while preserving much of the original performance. When combined with architectural replacements, meta-learning, or task-aware layer matching, KD can be adapted to diverse settings (on-device inference, federated systems, data-scarce environments) and modalities. However, its effectiveness depends on choices such as which signals to transfer, how to handle imperfect teachers, and how to preserve rare or low-frequency behaviors; addressing these challenges is necessary for robust practical adoption.

papers_seen.author: Kidd
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable approach for compressing large deep learning models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. Modern KD goes beyond matching logits: it includes feature- and representation-level transfers, multi-teacher and self-distillation strategies, and workflows that integrate augmentation, data-free synthesis, pruning, and quantization to meet latency, memory, and privacy requirements. Practical success depends on matching distillation technique to deployment objectives, careful design of layer mappings and loss terms, attention to teacher quality and data availability, and combinations with other compression tools to preserve robustness and generalization.

papers_seen.author: Lawrence
papers_seen.title: Practical Benefits and Cautions of Knowledge Distillation for NLP Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach to compressing large deep and language models into smaller, faster models suitable for deployment. When applied thoughtfully—using techniques such as data augmentation, multi-teacher training, teacher optimization, or data-free procedures—KD can preserve much of the teacher's utility while reducing inference cost and memory. However, distillation can transfer or amplify undesirable properties of teachers (e.g., biases), and its success depends on choices like which teacher knowledge to transfer and which training samples to use. I argue KD is a powerful tool for NLP model compression but must be combined with targeted strategies for robustness, fairness, privacy, and sample selection to realize its full benefits in practice.

papers_seen.author: Dudley
papers_seen.title: Attention-Guided Answer Distillation for Machine Reading Comprehension
papers_seen.abstract: Despite that current reading comprehension systems have achieved significant advancements, their promising performances are often obtained at the cost of making an ensemble of numerous models. Besides, existing approaches are also vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper tackles these problems by leveraging knowledge distillation, which aims to transfer knowledge from an ensemble model to a single model. We first demonstrate that vanilla knowledge distillation applied to answer span prediction is effective for reading comprehension systems. We then propose two novel approaches that not only penalize the prediction on confusing answers but also guide the training with alignment information distilled from the ensemble. Experiments show that our best student model has only a slight drop of 0.4% F1 on the SQuAD test set compared to the ensemble teacher, while running 12x faster during inference. It even outperforms the teacher on adversarial SQuAD datasets and NarrativeQA benchmark.

papers_seen.author: Zamora
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing teacher models into smaller, cheaper students by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. The family of KD methods includes soft-target (logit) matching, feature- and layer-wise alignment, relational and module-level transfer, data-free or zero-shot synthesis, and integration with architecture search or federated training. Practical deployments balance what is transferred with student capacity, data availability, privacy constraints, and device heterogeneity; empirical work shows KD often preserves much of teacher performance while enabling lower latency, smaller models, and domain specialization, but open challenges remain around robustness, domain shift, and principled selection of distilled signals.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Path to Deployable Deep Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical framework for producing compact, faster models that retain much of the capability of larger teachers. Beyond simple logit matching, modern KD leverages internal representation transfer, selective data strategies, and integration with pruning, architecture search, or federated protocols to meet latency, privacy, and device-heterogeneity constraints. When applied thoughtfully, KD enables efficient deployment across modalities while posing clear methodological trade-offs and open challenges that guide future research.

papers_seen.author: Morales
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical Tool for Compressing and Adapting Deep and NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for producing smaller models that retain much of the performance and useful behavior of larger teachers. KD supports a spectrum of deployment goals — reduced latency and memory, domain adaptation, privacy-aware training, and robustness improvements — and works best when combined with complementary techniques (e.g., layer mapping, feature matching, synthetic-data generation, pruning, or quantization). However, KD is not a universal solution: outcomes depend on teacher quality, what signals are transferred, data fidelity, and design choices that align distilled knowledge to the downstream task. Practical adoption therefore requires principled pipeline choices and awareness of KD failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Extract the Knowledge of Graph Neural Networks and Go Beyond it: An Effective Knowledge Distillation Framework
papers_seen.abstract: Semi-supervised learning on graphs is an important problem in the machine learning area. In recent years, state-of-the-art classification methods based on graph neural networks (GNNs) have shown their superiority over traditional ones such as label propagation. However, the sophisticated architectures of these neural models will lead to a complex prediction mechanism, which could not make full use of valuable prior knowledge lying in the data, e.g., structurally correlated nodes tend to have the same class. In this paper, we propose a framework based on knowledge distillation to address the above issues. Our framework extracts the knowledge of an arbitrary learned GNN model (teacher model), and injects it into a well-designed student model. The student model is built with two simple prediction mechanisms, i.e., label propagation and feature transformation, which naturally preserves structure-based and feature-based prior knowledge, respectively. In specific, we design the student model as a trainable combination of parameterized label propagation and feature transformation modules. As a result, the learned student can benefit from both prior knowledge and the knowledge in GNN teachers for more effective predictions. Moreover, the learned student model has a more interpretable prediction process than GNNs. We conduct experiments on five public benchmark datasets and employ seven GNN models including GCN, GAT, APPNP, SAGE, SGC, GCNII and GLP as the teacher models. Experimental results show that the learned student model can consistently outperform its corresponding teacher model by 1.4% - 4.7% on average. Code and data are available at https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/CPF

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: What We Know
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical suite of techniques that transfers information from large teacher models to smaller students to enable efficient deployment. In practice KD spans matching teacher outputs (soft logits), aligning intermediate representations, specialized layer- and channel-level transfers, and workflows that combine distillation with pruning, quantization, or synthetic-data strategies. KD delivers substantial reductions in compute, memory, and latency while often improving student generalization, but its success depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacity, and how to handle data or domain shifts. Open issues include robustness under distributional heterogeneity, preserving rare-token or fine-grained behavior in sequence models, and distillation without original training data.

papers_seen.author: Abbott
papers_seen.title: Compressing Deep Graph Neural Networks via Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep graph neural networks (GNNs) have been shown to be expressive for modeling graph-structured data. Nevertheless, the over-stacked architecture of deep graph models makes it difficult to deploy and rapidly test on mobile or embedded systems. To compress over-stacked GNNs, knowledge distillation via a teacher-student architecture turns out to be an effective technique, where the key step is to measure the discrepancy between teacher and student networks with predefined distance functions. However, using the same distance for graphs of various structures may be unfit, and the optimal distance formulation is hard to determine. To tackle these problems, we propose a novel Adversarial Knowledge Distillation framework for graph models named GraphAKD, which adversarially trains a discriminator and a generator to adaptively detect and decrease the discrepancy. Specifically, noticing that the well-captured inter-node and inter-class correlations favor the success of deep GNNs, we propose to criticize the inherited knowledge from node-level and class-level views with a trainable discriminator. The discriminator distinguishes between teacher knowledge and what the student inherits, while the student GNN works as a generator and aims to fool the discriminator. To our best knowledge, GraphAKD is the first to introduce adversarial training to knowledge distillation in graph domains. Experiments on node-level and graph-level classification benchmarks demonstrate that GraphAKD improves the student performance by a large margin. The results imply that GraphAKD can precisely transfer knowledge from a complicated teacher GNN to a compact student GNN.

papers_seen.author: Walton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential, Practical Strategy for Compressing Deep Models in NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques are indispensable for deploying high-capacity deep and language models in resource-constrained settings. By transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teachers to smaller students, practitioners can achieve large reductions in model size and latency while retaining most task performance. However, realizing these gains reliably requires attention to what is transferred (logits, features, relations), how teachers and data are chosen, and hardware- or deployment-aware compression strategies.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Flexible Path to Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile and production-ready approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Across vision, graph, and language tasks, distillation techniques can be adapted to preserve logits, features, or relational structure, and can be extended into online, multi-teacher, privacy-aware, and domain-adaptive settings. Effective use of distillation requires attention to what is transferred (soft labels, intermediate representations, relational signals), how teachers and students are aligned (projectors, input alignment, progressive replacement), and operational constraints (scalability, privacy, domain shift). When these design choices are matched to the task, distillation yields strong trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and resource use.

papers_seen.author: Leonard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Core for Compressing Deep and NLP Models: Strengths, Limits, and How to Apply It
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large deep and language models into smaller, deployable students. When applied thoughtfully—combining logits and representation matching, adapting teacher and student designs, and addressing data- or privacy-constrained settings—KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while retaining much of teacher performance. However, KD is not a cure-all: optimization difficulties, teacher imperfections, data mismatch, and distributional limits require targeted strategies (e.g., feature-aware losses, data-free synthesis, online or multi-teacher schemes) to make distillation robust and production-ready.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Channel Distillation: Channel-Wise Attention for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is to transfer the knowledge from the data learned by the teacher network to the student network, so that the student has the advantage of less parameters and less calculations, and the accuracy is close to the teacher. In this paper, we propose a new distillation method, which contains two transfer distillation strategies and a loss decay strategy. The first transfer strategy is based on channel-wise attention, called Channel Distillation (CD). CD transfers the channel information from the teacher to the student. The second is Guided Knowledge Distillation (GKD). Unlike Knowledge Distillation (KD), which allows the student to mimic each sample's prediction distribution of the teacher, GKD only enables the student to mimic the correct output of the teacher. The last part is Early Decay Teacher (EDT). During the training process, we gradually decay the weight of the distillation loss. The purpose is to enable the student to gradually control the optimization rather than the teacher. Our proposed method is evaluated on ImageNet and CIFAR100. On ImageNet, we achieve 27.68% of top-1 error with ResNet18, which outperforms state-of-the-art methods. On CIFAR100, we achieve surprising result that the student outperforms the teacher. Code is available at https://github.com/zhouzaida/channel-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression strategies enable smaller, faster models to inherit performance from larger teachers by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or ensemble knowledge. Techniques range from logit-based soft-target distillation to feature- and attention-level mimicry, multi-teacher and task-adaptive pipelines, and methods that relax the need for original training data or strong teachers. Across computer vision and natural language processing tasks, distilled students can approach teacher accuracy while drastically reducing parameters and latency; complementary strategies such as careful pre-training of compact models and architecture search further improve trade-offs between efficiency and effectiveness. Key challenges remain in preserving rare-token behavior, aligning heterogeneous teacher–student inputs, and ensuring privacy and robustness during compression.

papers_seen.author: Kim
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When paired with representation-aware objectives, careful pre-training of compact models, and safeguards for robustness and privacy, KD enables production-ready reductions in latency, memory, and energy while retaining much of a teacher's performance. I argue that KD should be treated as a central tool in model-compression pipelines, not as a single recipe but as a family of methods to be combined with task-aware design choices for reliable deployment.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Understanding BERT Rankers Under Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep language models such as BERT pre-trained on large corpus have given a huge performance boost to the state-of-the-art information retrieval ranking systems. Knowledge embedded in such models allows them to pick up complex matching signals between passages and queries. However, the high computation cost during inference limits their deployment in real-world search scenarios. In this paper, we study if and how the knowledge for search within BERT can be transferred to a smaller ranker through distillation. Our experiments demonstrate that it is crucial to use a proper distillation procedure, which produces up to nine times speedup while preserving the state-of-the-art performance.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: BAM! Born-Again Multi-Task Networks for Natural Language Understanding
papers_seen.abstract: It can be challenging to train multi-task neural networks that outperform or even match their single-task counterparts. To help address this, we propose using knowledge distillation where single-task models teach a multi-task model. We enhance this training with teacher annealing, a novel method that gradually transitions the model from distillation to supervised learning, helping the multi-task model surpass its single-task teachers. We evaluate our approach by multi-task fine-tuning BERT on the GLUE benchmark. Our method consistently improves over standard single-task and multi-task training.

papers_seen.author: Whitehead
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller student models to reduce computation, memory, and latency while retaining much of the original performance. KD encompasses a family of techniques — matching soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, using multi-stage or curriculum schemes, and combining distillation with other compression methods — and is widely used for deploying models in resource-constrained or privacy-sensitive settings. Success depends on matching distillation objectives and data strategies to deployment goals and student capacity.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Linkless Link Prediction via Relational Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown exceptional performance in the task of link prediction. Despite their effectiveness, the high latency brought by non-trivial neighborhood data dependency limits GNNs in practical deployments. Conversely, the known efficient MLPs are much less effective than GNNs due to the lack of relational knowledge. In this work, to combine the advantages of GNNs and MLPs, we start with exploring direct knowledge distillation (KD) methods for link prediction, i.e., predicted logit-based matching and node representation-based matching. Upon observing direct KD analogs do not perform well for link prediction, we propose a relational KD framework, Linkless Link Prediction (LLP), to distill knowledge for link prediction with MLPs. Unlike simple KD methods that match independent link logits or node representations, LLP distills relational knowledge that is centered around each (anchor) node to the student MLP. Specifically, we propose rank-based matching and distribution-based matching strategies that complement each other. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LLP boosts the link prediction performance of MLPs with significant margins, and even outperforms the teacher GNNs on 7 out of 8 benchmarks. LLP also achieves a 70.68x speedup in link prediction inference compared to GNNs on the large-scale OGB dataset.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques have matured into a diverse set of approaches that trade off capacity, latency, and privacy to deploy high-performing deep models in constrained settings. Methods operate at different places in the training pipeline: compressing via soft-targets, transferring intermediate representations, searching or adapting compact architectures, or avoiding access to original data. Work across modalities (vision, language, graphs, generative models, and medical imaging) shows that careful choice of what to transfer (logits, relations, feature directions, layer mappings) and how to transfer it (attention, contrastive alignment, adversarial generators, or task-aware filters) determines final student performance. Practical concerns such as domain adaptation, federated and heterogeneous-device settings, and data augmentation interact strongly with distillation design choices. The literature suggests a clear pattern: representation-level and layer-aware transfers often outperform naive logits-only approaches for structured or pre-trained models, while teacher-free, data-free, and communication-efficient variants enable distillation under realistic deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression methods aim to transfer performance and representational properties from large, expensive models to smaller, efficient ones. Across tasks in vision, language, graph learning, and generative modeling, researchers have developed strategies that extend beyond matching final logits: layer-wise and representation matching, many-to-many layer alignment, data-free distillation, private/distilled deployment, multi-teacher and self-distillation schemes, and task-adaptive compression. These approaches trade off fidelity, privacy, and computational cost, and they have been shown to enable real-world deployment of pretrained language models and other deep systems while revealing open challenges in distribution shift, heterogeneous data, and preserving inductive biases.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Towards Model Agnostic Federated Learning Using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Is it possible to design an universal API for federated learning using which an ad-hoc group of data-holders (agents) collaborate with each other and perform federated learning? Such an API would necessarily need to be model-agnostic i.e. make no assumption about the model architecture being used by the agents, and also cannot rely on having representative public data at hand. Knowledge distillation (KD) is the obvious tool of choice to design such protocols. However, surprisingly, we show that most natural KD-based federated learning protocols have poor performance.   To investigate this, we propose a new theoretical framework, Federated Kernel ridge regression, which can capture both model heterogeneity as well as data heterogeneity. Our analysis shows that the degradation is largely due to a fundamental limitation of knowledge distillation under data heterogeneity. We further validate our framework by analyzing and designing new protocols based on KD. Their performance on real world experiments using neural networks, though still unsatisfactory, closely matches our theoretical predictions.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers information from larger teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost while retaining much of the teacher's performance. KD methods operate at multiple granularities (soft-label/logit matching, intermediate-feature imitation, module- or layer-wise mapping) and appear across domains including NLP, vision, multimodal, federated, and graph settings. Practical pipelines combine KD with data strategies, teacher adaptation, and complementary compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search), but open challenges remain around data heterogeneity, teacher imperfections, and preserving properties such as low-frequency token fidelity, robustness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Abbott
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Issues
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, speech, and NLP. Approaches vary from traditional teacher-to-student soft-label transfer to data-free (zero-shot) distillation, online and mutual distillation among peers, meta-learned teachers, and internal-representation matching. Empirical work shows KD can improve student generalization, speed, and footprint but also introduces dataset-specific artifacts (e.g., degraded modeling of low-frequency tokens) and optimization mismatches that require complementary strategies such as exposing raw data, augmentations, adaptive teacher selection, or distillation of intermediate representations. Practical systems (federated or large-scale distributed training) benefit from variants like online or zero-shot distillation to respect privacy and device heterogeneity, while research continues to study why KD works and how to align teacher and student beyond output probabilities.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Practical and Responsible Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach to compressing large models into smaller, faster ones for deployment in resource-constrained settings. However, successful distillation requires attention to optimization dynamics, representation alignment, data availability and privacy, robustness, and social biases. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a suite of complementary techniques — including feature mimicking, input alignment, multi-teacher curricula, data-free synthesis, and adversarially-aware training — and outlines concrete best practices for applying KD in deep learning and NLP to maximize utility while minimizing harms.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Improved Accuracy in Spoken Question Answering
papers_seen.abstract: Spoken question answering (SQA) is a challenging task that requires the machine to fully understand the complex spoken documents. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) plays a significant role in the development of QA systems. However, the recent work shows that ASR systems generate highly noisy transcripts, which critically limit the capability of machine comprehension on the SQA task. To address the issue, we present a novel distillation framework. Specifically, we devise a training strategy to perform knowledge distillation (KD) from spoken documents and written counterparts. Our work makes a step towards distilling knowledge from the language model as a supervision signal to lead to better student accuracy by reducing the misalignment between automatic and manual transcriptions. Experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art language models on the Spoken-SQuAD dataset.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Improved Feature Distillation via Projector Ensemble
papers_seen.abstract: In knowledge distillation, previous feature distillation methods mainly focus on the design of loss functions and the selection of the distilled layers, while the effect of the feature projector between the student and the teacher remains under-explored. In this paper, we first discuss a plausible mechanism of the projector with empirical evidence and then propose a new feature distillation method based on a projector ensemble for further performance improvement. We observe that the student network benefits from a projector even if the feature dimensions of the student and the teacher are the same. Training a student backbone without a projector can be considered as a multi-task learning process, namely achieving discriminative feature extraction for classification and feature matching between the student and the teacher for distillation at the same time. We hypothesize and empirically verify that without a projector, the student network tends to overfit the teacher's feature distributions despite having different architecture and weights initialization. This leads to degradation on the quality of the student's deep features that are eventually used in classification. Adding a projector, on the other hand, disentangles the two learning tasks and helps the student network to focus better on the main feature extraction task while still being able to utilize teacher features as a guidance through the projector. Motivated by the positive effect of the projector in feature distillation, we propose an ensemble of projectors to further improve the quality of student features. Experimental results on different datasets with a series of teacher-student pairs illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

papers_seen.author: Daniels
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, faster students by transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels alone. Methods range from matching softened logits to imitating internal representations, attention maps, or channel-wise activations, and can be combined with quantization, low-precision numerics, architecture-aware design, and data- or teacher-aware training regimes. In practice, distillation is a multifaceted toolkit that must be tailored to deployment goals (latency, memory, domain adaptation, privacy, robustness), and remaining challenges include principled sample selection, representation alignment across heterogeneous architectures, and preserving robustness and fairness under compression.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Graph-less Neural Networks: Teaching Old MLPs New Tricks via Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are popular for graph machine learning and have shown great results on wide node classification tasks. Yet, they are less popular for practical deployments in the industry owing to their scalability challenges incurred by data dependency. Namely, GNN inference depends on neighbor nodes multiple hops away from the target, and fetching them burdens latency-constrained applications. Existing inference acceleration methods like pruning and quantization can speed up GNNs by reducing Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) operations, but the improvements are limited given the data dependency is not resolved. Conversely, multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) have no graph dependency and infer much faster than GNNs, even though they are less accurate than GNNs for node classification in general. Motivated by these complementary strengths and weaknesses, we bring GNNs and MLPs together via knowledge distillation (KD). Our work shows that the performance of MLPs can be improved by large margins with GNN KD. We call the distilled MLPs Graph-less Neural Networks (GLNNs) as they have no inference graph dependency. We show that GLNNs with competitive accuracy infer faster than GNNs by 146X-273X and faster than other acceleration methods by 14X-27X. Under a production setting involving both transductive and inductive predictions across 7 datasets, GLNN accuracies improve over stand-alone MLPs by 12.36% on average and match GNNs on 6/7 datasets. Comprehensive analysis shows when and why GLNNs can achieve competitive accuracies to GNNs and suggests GLNN as a handy choice for latency-constrained applications.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: A Practical, Multifaceted Position on Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central, practical tool for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as a multifaceted framework—combining soft-label supervision, intermediate representation matching, data- and task-aware training, and architecture-aware design—distillation reliably yields compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting deployment constraints. However, distillation must be applied carefully: teacher imperfections, low-frequency token behavior, data scarcity, and domain shifts can undermine student quality unless addressed via targeted strategies such as exposing raw data, tailoring teacher signals, and integrating complementary compression methods. With careful engineering and principled choices about what and how to transfer, distillation enables high-performing, efficient models across vision and language tasks.

papers_seen.author: Hoffman
papers_seen.title: Federated Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Distributed learning frameworks often rely on exchanging model parameters across workers, instead of revealing their raw data. A prime example is federated learning that exchanges the gradients or weights of each neural network model. Under limited communication resources, however, such a method becomes extremely costly particularly for modern deep neural networks having a huge number of model parameters. In this regard, federated distillation (FD) is a compelling distributed learning solution that only exchanges the model outputs whose dimensions are commonly much smaller than the model sizes (e.g., 10 labels in the MNIST dataset). The goal of this chapter is to provide a deep understanding of FD while demonstrating its communication efficiency and applicability to a variety of tasks. To this end, towards demystifying the operational principle of FD, the first part of this chapter provides a novel asymptotic analysis for two foundational algorithms of FD, namely knowledge distillation (KD) and co-distillation (CD), by exploiting the theory of neural tangent kernel (NTK). Next, the second part elaborates on a baseline implementation of FD for a classification task, and illustrates its performance in terms of accuracy and communication efficiency compared to FL. Lastly, to demonstrate the applicability of FD to various distributed learning tasks and environments, the third part presents two selected applications, namely FD over asymmetric uplink-and-downlink wireless channels and FD for reinforcement learning.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers behavior from large teacher models into smaller student models to reduce latency, memory, and computation while retaining much of the teacher's performance. Across vision, language, and graph domains, KD has been applied as logit matching, intermediate-feature alignment, adversarial transfer, and data- or task-aware synthesis. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often acts both as a source of extra task signal and as a regularizer; practical systems combine KD with pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation, and data strategies to meet deployment constraints. Important open issues include data heterogeneity, teacher–student capacity mismatch, privacy-preserving releases, and closing remaining gaps in robustness and domain generalization.

papers_seen.author: Koch
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques aim to transfer useful knowledge from larger, expensive models to smaller, more efficient ones so that deployed systems retain high performance under resource constraints. Approaches span logit-level supervision, feature- and layer-level matching, progressive module replacement, and data-augmentation or data-free strategies. Applications include compressing large language models, accelerating inference on edge devices, enabling multi-task and federated learning, and improving robustness or generalization. Practical deployments often combine KD with quantization, architecture design, or task-aware selection of teacher signals to balance fidelity and efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Hoffman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Path to Efficient Deep and NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation provides a pragmatic and versatile set of techniques to compress large neural models into compact, faster students while retaining much of their performance. Across NLP and vision, modern distillation variants — including multi-teacher pipelines, self-distillation, teacher optimization, and task-aware layer alignment — address core challenges such as capacity gaps and task-specific redundancy. When combined with complementary compression strategies (pruning, low-precision arithmetic, architecture search), distillation enables deployment of high-performing models under tight resource or latency constraints.

papers_seen.author: Lawrence
papers_seen.title: Practical Benefits and Cautions of Knowledge Distillation for NLP Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach to compressing large deep and language models into smaller, faster models suitable for deployment. When applied thoughtfully—using techniques such as data augmentation, multi-teacher training, teacher optimization, or data-free procedures—KD can preserve much of the teacher's utility while reducing inference cost and memory. However, distillation can transfer or amplify undesirable properties of teachers (e.g., biases), and its success depends on choices like which teacher knowledge to transfer and which training samples to use. I argue KD is a powerful tool for NLP model compression but must be combined with targeted strategies for robustness, fairness, privacy, and sample selection to realize its full benefits in practice.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer predictive behavior and internal structure from larger, often pre-trained teacher models into smaller, efficient student models in order to reduce latency, memory, and deployment cost while retaining task performance. Methods span matching soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, attention- or relation-based feature matching, curriculum strategies for progressively harder supervision, and task- or data-aware architecture search. Practical success depends on student capacity, availability and quality of data, whether the student itself is pre-trained, and choices about what to transfer; open challenges include preserving fairness and robustness, aligning heterogeneous architectures, and operating under privacy or data-limited conditions.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Flexible Path to Compact and Robust NLP and Deep Learning Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and versatile set of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster ones while retaining most of their performance. Distillation methods can be adapted to structural compression, domain adaptation, low-data or no-data scenarios, and different model families (transformers, convolutional nets, graph models). A pragmatic compression strategy combines well-chosen distillation objectives with complementary methods (pruning, architecture transformations, multi-teacher supervision, or data-generation) to meet deployment constraints without sacrificing reliability.

papers_seen.author: Kim
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When paired with representation-aware objectives, careful pre-training of compact models, and safeguards for robustness and privacy, KD enables production-ready reductions in latency, memory, and energy while retaining much of a teacher's performance. I argue that KD should be treated as a central tool in model-compression pipelines, not as a single recipe but as a family of methods to be combined with task-aware design choices for reliable deployment.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: AlphaNet: Improved Training of Supernets with Alpha-Divergence
papers_seen.abstract: Weight-sharing neural architecture search (NAS) is an effective technique for automating efficient neural architecture design. Weight-sharing NAS builds a supernet that assembles all the architectures as its sub-networks and jointly trains the supernet with the sub-networks. The success of weight-sharing NAS heavily relies on distilling the knowledge of the supernet to the sub-networks. However, we find that the widely used distillation divergence, i.e., KL divergence, may lead to student sub-networks that over-estimate or under-estimate the uncertainty of the teacher supernet, leading to inferior performance of the sub-networks. In this work, we propose to improve the supernet training with a more generalized alpha-divergence. By adaptively selecting the alpha-divergence, we simultaneously prevent the over-estimation or under-estimation of the uncertainty of the teacher model. We apply the proposed alpha-divergence based supernets training to both slimmable neural networks and weight-sharing NAS, and demonstrate significant improvements. Specifically, our discovered model family, AlphaNet, outperforms prior-art models on a wide range of FLOPs regimes, including BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS. We achieve ImageNet top-1 accuracy of 80.0% with only 444M FLOPs. Our code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/AlphaNet.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across computer vision and NLP, practitioners use KD to reduce inference cost, enable on-device deployment, and adapt large pretrained models to constrained settings. KD techniques vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational signals), how training data are handled (real, augmented, synthesized, or none), and how teachers and students are aligned architecturally and procedurally. When design choices are matched to the task and constraints, KD enables substantial compression with modest performance loss; however, challenges remain for heterogeneous architectures, generative tasks, privacy-sensitive settings, and preserving rare-token or low-frequency behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Lawrence
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge From a Deep Pose Regressor Network
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a novel method to distill knowledge from a deep pose regressor network for efficient Visual Odometry (VO). Standard distillation relies on "dark knowledge" for successful knowledge transfer. As this knowledge is not available in pose regression and the teacher prediction is not always accurate, we propose to emphasize the knowledge transfer only when we trust the teacher. We achieve this by using teacher loss as a confidence score which places variable relative importance on the teacher prediction. We inject this confidence score to the main training task via Attentive Imitation Loss (AIL) and when learning the intermediate representation of the teacher through Attentive Hint Training (AHT) approach. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work which successfully distill the knowledge from a deep pose regression network. Our evaluation on the KITTI and Malaga dataset shows that we can keep the student prediction close to the teacher with up to 92.95% parameter reduction and 2.12x faster in computation time.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression encompass a family of methods that transfer information from larger, high-capacity models (teachers) to smaller, efficient models (students). These approaches aim to retain predictive performance while reducing model size, latency, or enabling deployment under privacy or communication constraints. Recent work broadens distillation beyond logits to intermediate features, attention maps, multi-teacher setups, and data-limited or privacy-preserving regimes, producing task- and domain-aware compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: FedZKT: Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer towards Resource-Constrained Federated Learning with Heterogeneous On-Device Models
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning enables multiple distributed devices to collaboratively learn a shared prediction model without centralizing their on-device data. Most of the current algorithms require comparable individual efforts for local training with the same structure and size of on-device models, which, however, impedes participation from resource-constrained devices. Given the widespread yet heterogeneous devices nowadays, in this paper, we propose an innovative federated learning framework with heterogeneous on-device models through Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer, named by FedZKT. Specifically, FedZKT allows devices to independently determine the on-device models upon their local resources. To achieve knowledge transfer across these heterogeneous on-device models, a zero-shot distillation approach is designed without any prerequisites for private on-device data, which is contrary to certain prior research based on a public dataset or a pre-trained data generator. Moreover, this compute-intensive distillation task is assigned to the server to allow the participation of resource-constrained devices, where a generator is adversarially learned with the ensemble of collected on-device models. The distilled central knowledge is then sent back in the form of the corresponding on-device model parameters, which can be easily absorbed on the device side. Extensive experimental studies demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of FedZKT towards on-device knowledge agnostic, on-device model heterogeneity, and other challenging federated learning scenarios, such as heterogeneous on-device data and straggler effects.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: On Representation Knowledge Distillation for Graph Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a learning paradigm for boosting resource-efficient graph neural networks (GNNs) using more expressive yet cumbersome teacher models. Past work on distillation for GNNs proposed the Local Structure Preserving loss (LSP), which matches local structural relationships defined over edges across the student and teacher's node embeddings. This paper studies whether preserving the global topology of how the teacher embeds graph data can be a more effective distillation objective for GNNs, as real-world graphs often contain latent interactions and noisy edges. We propose Graph Contrastive Representation Distillation (G-CRD), which uses contrastive learning to implicitly preserve global topology by aligning the student node embeddings to those of the teacher in a shared representation space. Additionally, we introduce an expanded set of benchmarks on large-scale real-world datasets where the performance gap between teacher and student GNNs is non-negligible. Experiments across 4 datasets and 14 heterogeneous GNN architectures show that G-CRD consistently boosts the performance and robustness of lightweight GNNs, outperforming LSP (and a global structure preserving variant of LSP) as well as baselines from 2D computer vision. An analysis of the representational similarity among teacher and student embedding spaces reveals that G-CRD balances preserving local and global relationships, while structure preserving approaches are best at preserving one or the other. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns

papers_seen.author: Peters
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large teacher models into smaller student models by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or other forms of learned structure so students retain much of teacher performance while reducing inference cost. KD has evolved from simple soft-target matching to a broad toolkit that includes feature- and representation-level objectives, multi-teacher schemes, data- and privacy-aware variants, and combinations with pruning or quantization. Practical application requires task- and deployment-aware choices that balance accuracy, latency, data availability, and social/robustness concerns.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers with Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of unifying knowledge from a set of classifiers with different architectures and target classes into a single classifier, given only a generic set of unlabelled data. We call this problem Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers (UHC). This problem is motivated by scenarios where data is collected from multiple sources, but the sources cannot share their data, e.g., due to privacy concerns, and only privately trained models can be shared. In addition, each source may not be able to gather data to train all classes due to data availability at each source, and may not be able to train the same classification model due to different computational resources. To tackle this problem, we propose a generalisation of knowledge distillation to merge HCs. We derive a probabilistic relation between the outputs of HCs and the probability over all classes. Based on this relation, we propose two classes of methods based on cross-entropy minimisation and matrix factorisation, which allow us to estimate soft labels over all classes from unlabelled samples and use them in lieu of ground truth labels to train a unified classifier. Our extensive experiments on ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets show that our approaches significantly outperform a naive extension of distillation and can achieve almost the same accuracy as classifiers that are trained in a centralised, supervised manner.

papers_seen.author: Chapman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, faster students by transferring useful predictive behavior, representations, or inductive biases. A diverse set of distillation strategies—matching soft logits, aligning intermediate features or attention maps, self-distillation, multi-teacher schemes, data-free synthesis, and task-aware adaptations—has been developed to preserve performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Practice-oriented work emphasizes matching the distillation technique to the task, addressing data or privacy limits via synthetic examples or adversarial generation, and combining distillation with architecture and optimization adjustments to close remaining gaps. Empirical successes across language, vision, speech, graphs, and ranking systems show substantial speed and size improvements, though limits remain around distribution shift, teacher–student mismatch, and heterogeneous or federated data settings.

papers_seen.author: Liu
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Strategy for Compressing NLP Models: Benefits, Limits, and Practical Recipes
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable ones. In NLP, KD enables retaining much of the teacher model's linguistic capability while reducing storage and inference cost. Effective compression with KD requires more than mimicking final outputs: it benefits from aligning internal representations, task-aware layer mapping, and handling data or privacy constraints with synthetic or metadata-driven techniques. However, KD is not a panacea — distributional heterogeneity, privacy, and mismatches between teacher and student capacity pose real limits that must be mitigated by careful method design and evaluation.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques reduce the size, memory, and inference cost of large neural networks by transferring knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller student models. Across tasks and modalities—classification, detection, generative modeling, retrieval, and NLP—research has developed logits-based, feature-based, and task-adapted distillation strategies, multi-teacher and ensemble approaches, privacy- and communication-conscious protocols for distributed settings, and teacher-optimization/meta-learning variants. These methods trade off fidelity to teacher behavior with student capacity, expose failure modes (e.g., transfer of low-frequency lexical mistakes or overfitting of student features), and introduce remedies such as selective sample distillation, feature projectors, adversarially-informed samples, and staged or multi-teacher curricula. While KD consistently improves compact models compared to training from scratch and enables deployment on resource-constrained platforms, open issues remain in robustness, task-specific alignment, and distillation under data heterogeneity.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Trade-offs, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) trains compact student models by transferring information from larger teacher models, enabling deployment under computation, memory, or latency constraints. Across vision, speech, language, and recommendation systems, KD takes many forms — logit matching, feature mimicking, ensemble compression, and data-free synthesis — and is often combined with model pruning, architectural simplification, or curriculum strategies. Effective distillation requires choices about what to transfer (soft targets vs. intermediate features), how to supply or synthesize data, and how to schedule or regularize training; these choices shape outcomes in accuracy, robustness, interpretability, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across vision, speech, and language tasks, KD has expanded from simple logit matching to a rich toolbox including feature- and layer-level imitation, self- and progressive-distillation, ensemble compression, data-free or zero-shot approaches, and federated protocols. Empirical work shows KD can yield compact models that retain much of teacher performance while reducing inference cost, but practical success depends on design choices about what to transfer, how to supply or synthesize data, and how to handle teacher–student mismatches and optimization challenges.

papers_seen.author: Nguyen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical and Multifaceted Tool for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. Across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks, KD enables substantial reductions in memory and inference cost while retaining much of the teacher's performance. However, KD is not a silver bullet: its effectiveness depends on choices of teacher/student architecture, what is distilled (logits, layers, attention, representations), the optimization and data used for distillation, and constraints such as privacy or fairness. Carefully combining KD with techniques like multi-teacher schedules, layer-mapping strategies, task-adaptive compression, and privacy-preserving perturbations yields the best trade-offs for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Barnes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practical Patterns, and Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses high-capacity teacher models into smaller student models by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. Across vision and language, distillation strategies—matching logits, internal features, attention or relational structure, or using synthetic or public data—enable large reductions in model size and latency while preserving much of teacher performance. Practical deployments combine distillation with other compression tools, online or distributed training regimes, and privacy-aware variants, but face persistent challenges in aligning internal representations, retaining robustness and fairness, and operating under data or resource constraints.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer via Adversarial Belief Matching
papers_seen.abstract: Performing knowledge transfer from a large teacher network to a smaller student is a popular task in modern deep learning applications. However, due to growing dataset sizes and stricter privacy regulations, it is increasingly common not to have access to the data that was used to train the teacher. We propose a novel method which trains a student to match the predictions of its teacher without using any data or metadata. We achieve this by training an adversarial generator to search for images on which the student poorly matches the teacher, and then using them to train the student. Our resulting student closely approximates its teacher for simple datasets like SVHN, and on CIFAR10 we improve on the state-of-the-art for few-shot distillation (with 100 images per class), despite using no data. Finally, we also propose a metric to quantify the degree of belief matching between teacher and student in the vicinity of decision boundaries, and observe a significantly higher match between our zero-shot student and the teacher, than between a student distilled with real data and the teacher. Code available at: https://github.com/polo5/ZeroShotKnowledgeTransfer

Namely, GNN inference depends on neighbor nodes multiple hops away from the target, and fetching them burdens latency-constrained applications. Existing inference acceleration methods like pruning and quantization can speed up GNNs by reducing Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) operations, but the improvements are limited given the data dependency is not resolved. Conversely, multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) have no graph dependency and infer much faster than GNNs, even though they are less accurate than GNNs for node classification in general. Motivated by these complementary strengths and weaknesses, we bring GNNs and MLPs together via knowledge distillation (KD). Our work shows that the performance of MLPs can be improved by large margins with GNN KD. We call the distilled MLPs Graph-less Neural Networks (GLNNs) as they have no inference graph dependency. We show that GLNNs with competitive accuracy infer faster than GNNs by 146X-273X and faster than other acceleration methods by 14X-27X.
