papers_seen.author: Hickman
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques aim to transfer the predictive power of large, expensive models into smaller, faster models while retaining performance. Approaches vary from matching teacher outputs (soft labels) to aligning intermediate representations, leveraging data augmentation or synthesized data when real data are limited, and jointly optimizing architecture and distillation losses for task-adaptive compression. Advances address student–teacher capacity gaps, multi-teacher transfer, and domain or data scarcity; remaining challenges include transferring internal structure efficiently, generalization under distribution shifts, and designing teacher models that are optimized for downstream distillation.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Efficient and Responsible NLP and Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical, versatile approach for compressing large models and enabling deployment in resource-constrained environments. Beyond raw compression, KD supports domain adaptation, data-free scenarios, improved inference speed, and novel training regimes for specialized tasks. However, distillation is not a panacea: it can amplify teacher biases, interact with regularization techniques in subtle ways, and benefits most when combined with complementary methods such as architecture-aware training, generator-based sample synthesis, or instance-aware losses.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Cornerstone for Compressing Deep Models in NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic and broadly applicable strategy for compressing large deep models so they can be deployed under real-world constraints. By transferring predictive behavior or intermediate representations from a high-capacity teacher to a smaller student, KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while preserving much of the original performance. When combined with architectural replacements, meta-learning, or task-aware layer matching, KD can be adapted to diverse settings (on-device inference, federated systems, data-scarce environments) and modalities. However, its effectiveness depends on choices such as which signals to transfer, how to handle imperfect teachers, and how to preserve rare or low-frequency behaviors; addressing these challenges is necessary for robust practical adoption.

papers_seen.author: Novak
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Strategy for Compressing NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, production-ready approach that enables compact models to inherit much of the performance of large teachers while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints. When applied thoughtfully—using representation-level targets, projector layers, multi-teacher or curriculum schedules, and data-aware workflows—KD consistently outperforms training small models from scratch for many NLP tasks. However, KD is not a panacea: mismatches in capacity, teacher imperfections, data heterogeneity, and distributional shifts require targeted remedies and careful evaluation. This essay argues that KD should be treated as the practical core of model compression in deep learning and NLP, paired with specific design choices to mitigate its limits.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Towards Model Agnostic Federated Learning Using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Is it possible to design an universal API for federated learning using which an ad-hoc group of data-holders (agents) collaborate with each other and perform federated learning? Such an API would necessarily need to be model-agnostic i.e. make no assumption about the model architecture being used by the agents, and also cannot rely on having representative public data at hand. Knowledge distillation (KD) is the obvious tool of choice to design such protocols. However, surprisingly, we show that most natural KD-based federated learning protocols have poor performance.   To investigate this, we propose a new theoretical framework, Federated Kernel ridge regression, which can capture both model heterogeneity as well as data heterogeneity. Our analysis shows that the degradation is largely due to a fundamental limitation of knowledge distillation under data heterogeneity. We further validate our framework by analyzing and designing new protocols based on KD. Their performance on real world experiments using neural networks, though still unsatisfactory, closely matches our theoretical predictions.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques aim to transfer predictive performance and internal representations from large, expensive teacher models to smaller, faster student models. Work in this area spans theoretical analyses, practical compression recipes for language and vision models, approaches that avoid access to original training data, and methods that target robustness, privacy, or device heterogeneity. The field balances trade-offs among student capacity, teacher imperfection, data availability, and downstream task requirements, producing a range of techniques—logit-level distillation, layer-wise and module-level matching, progressive replacement, data-free generation, and combined compression with low-precision numerics—that are evaluated across tasks from BERT compression to multimodal and 3D detection. This synthesis summarizes prevailing methods, motivations, and recurring challenges emerging from recent literature.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Efficient Transformer-based Large Scale Language Representations using Hardware-friendly Block Structured Pruning
papers_seen.abstract: Pre-trained large-scale language models have increasingly demonstrated high accuracy on many natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, the limited weight storage and computational speed on hardware platforms have impeded the popularity of pre-trained models, especially in the era of edge computing. In this work, we propose an efficient transformer-based large-scale language representation using hardware-friendly block structure pruning. We incorporate the reweighted group Lasso into block-structured pruning for optimization. Besides the significantly reduced weight storage and computation, the proposed approach achieves high compression rates. Experimental results on different models (BERT, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT) on the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark tasks show that we achieve up to 5.0x with zero or minor accuracy degradation on certain task(s). Our proposed method is also orthogonal to existing compact pre-trained language models such as DistilBERT using knowledge distillation, since a further 1.79x average compression rate can be achieved on top of DistilBERT with zero or minor accuracy degradation. It is suitable to deploy the final compressed model on resource-constrained edge devices.

papers_seen.author: Lawrence
papers_seen.title: Practical Benefits and Cautions of Knowledge Distillation for NLP Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach to compressing large deep and language models into smaller, faster models suitable for deployment. When applied thoughtfully—using techniques such as data augmentation, multi-teacher training, teacher optimization, or data-free procedures—KD can preserve much of the teacher's utility while reducing inference cost and memory. However, distillation can transfer or amplify undesirable properties of teachers (e.g., biases), and its success depends on choices like which teacher knowledge to transfer and which training samples to use. I argue KD is a powerful tool for NLP model compression but must be combined with targeted strategies for robustness, fairness, privacy, and sample selection to realize its full benefits in practice.

papers_seen.author: Osborne
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge from Deep Networks with Applications to Healthcare Domain
papers_seen.abstract: Exponential growth in Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) has resulted in new opportunities and urgent needs for discovery of meaningful data-driven representations and patterns of diseases in Computational Phenotyping research. Deep Learning models have shown superior performance for robust prediction in computational phenotyping tasks, but suffer from the issue of model interpretability which is crucial for clinicians involved in decision-making. In this paper, we introduce a novel knowledge-distillation approach called Interpretable Mimic Learning, to learn interpretable phenotype features for making robust prediction while mimicking the performance of deep learning models. Our framework uses Gradient Boosting Trees to learn interpretable features from deep learning models such as Stacked Denoising Autoencoder and Long Short-Term Memory. Exhaustive experiments on a real-world clinical time-series dataset show that our method obtains similar or better performance than the deep learning models, and it provides interpretable phenotypes for clinical decision making.

papers_seen.author: Carney
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a heuristic for shrinking large models into a broad set of techniques that enable smaller, faster, and often more robust or interpretable models for deep learning and NLP. Empirical and conceptual work shows KD operates through multiple mechanisms — soft-target regularization, transfer of internal representations, and optimization/inductive-bias alignment — and that design choices about what to transfer, how to supply training data, and how to reconcile teacher imperfections with student capacity determine success. KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful engineering (data selection, projectors, curriculum), but persistent challenges remain in heterogeneous architectures, data-limited or privacy-sensitive settings, and rare-token behavior.

papers_seen.author: Hurst
papers_seen.title: Contemporary Approaches and Applications of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger, more costly models to smaller, deployable models. Modern work expands beyond simple soft-label matching to include distillation of internal representations, feature-level imitation, privacy-preserving and data-free strategies, task-adaptive compression, and adaptations to specialized architectures (e.g., GANs, detectors, and transformers). These methods aim to preserve accuracy, robustness, and efficiency (compute, memory, or communication) while enabling deployment on resource-constrained devices or in privacy-sensitive and distributed settings.

papers_seen.author: Dudley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression: Strengths, Techniques, and Caveats
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, widely applicable approach for compressing models and transferring knowledge across architectures and modalities. By training compact students under the guidance of larger teachers, KD enables substantial reductions in memory, compute, and inference latency while retaining much of teacher performance. Its flexibility supports many modalities (vision, language, speech, 3D, and generative models) and deployment constraints, but realizing its benefits in practice requires careful choices about what to transfer (logits vs. features), which samples to use, and how to handle limited or private data.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Confidence-Aware Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is initially introduced to utilize additional supervision from a single teacher model for the student model training. To boost the student performance, some recent variants attempt to exploit diverse knowledge sources from multiple teachers. However, existing studies mainly integrate knowledge from diverse sources by averaging over multiple teacher predictions or combining them using other various label-free strategies, which may mislead student in the presence of low-quality teacher predictions. To tackle this problem, we propose Confidence-Aware Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (CA-MKD), which adaptively assigns sample-wise reliability for each teacher prediction with the help of ground-truth labels, with those teacher predictions close to one-hot labels assigned large weights. Besides, CA-MKD incorporates intermediate layers to stable the knowledge transfer process. Extensive experiments show that our CA-MKD consistently outperforms all compared state-of-the-art methods across various teacher-student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Rejuvenating Low-Frequency Words: Making the Most of Parallel Data in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is commonly used to construct synthetic data for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models. However, there exists a discrepancy on low-frequency words between the distilled and the original data, leading to more errors on predicting low-frequency words. To alleviate the problem, we directly expose the raw data into NAT by leveraging pretraining. By analyzing directed alignments, we found that KD makes low-frequency source words aligned with targets more deterministically but fails to align sufficient low-frequency words from target to source. Accordingly, we propose reverse KD to rejuvenate more alignments for low-frequency target words. To make the most of authentic and synthetic data, we combine these complementary approaches as a new training strategy for further boosting NAT performance. We conduct experiments on five translation benchmarks over two advanced architectures. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly and universally improve translation quality by reducing translation errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach achieves 28.2 and 33.9 BLEU points on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets, respectively. Our code, data, and trained models are available at \url{https://github.com/alphadl/RLFW-NAT}.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression strategies are widely used to produce smaller, faster models by transferring knowledge from larger or ensemble teachers to compact students. These techniques span supervised distillation, self-distillation, data-free and adversarial approaches, layer- and task-aware mappings, and distributed/online schemes. Empirical work shows KD can preserve much of teacher performance across modalities (classification, detection, generation, and language tasks) while enabling practical deployment; theoretical and practical challenges remain around data dependence, teacher imperfection, robustness, and optimal student–teacher alignment.

papers_seen.author: Roman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Practical Model Compression in NLP and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, multi-purpose strategy for compressing large deep models while preserving performance. KD can be adapted to constraints common in NLP deployment—limited compute, privacy restrictions, low-latency requirements, and robustness demands—by pairing standard teacher-student training with techniques such as feature-level matching, data augmentation, multi-teacher supervision, and teacher adaptation. Across domains (transformers for NLP, speech embeddings, graph models, generative models), KD consistently enables large reductions in model size or latency with modest accuracy loss, making it a primary method for productionization of deep models.

papers_seen.author: Arroyo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Scenarios, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques reduce the computational and storage footprint of large neural networks by transferring knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller students. Approaches span matching outputs (soft labels), transferring intermediate representations (feature or layer-wise distillation), adapting teacher selection and weighting, and operating under constraints such as missing original data, privacy, or multi-modal inputs. Practical work on language models, vision-language systems, and other domains highlights gains from task-aware selection of distilled information, architectural adapters between teacher and student, and advanced training schemes (e.g., adversarial sample generation, meta-learning of teachers). Empirical results and surveys show KD is versatile: it improves student accuracy over training from scratch, enables deployment in resource-constrained settings, and can be extended to preserve privacy and support domain adaptation, while theoretical and empirical analyses clarify when and why distillation helps and what challenges remain.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer via Adversarial Belief Matching
papers_seen.abstract: Performing knowledge transfer from a large teacher network to a smaller student is a popular task in modern deep learning applications. However, due to growing dataset sizes and stricter privacy regulations, it is increasingly common not to have access to the data that was used to train the teacher. We propose a novel method which trains a student to match the predictions of its teacher without using any data or metadata. We achieve this by training an adversarial generator to search for images on which the student poorly matches the teacher, and then using them to train the student. Our resulting student closely approximates its teacher for simple datasets like SVHN, and on CIFAR10 we improve on the state-of-the-art for few-shot distillation (with 100 images per class), despite using no data. Finally, we also propose a metric to quantify the degree of belief matching between teacher and student in the vicinity of decision boundaries, and observe a significantly higher match between our zero-shot student and the teacher, than between a student distilled with real data and the teacher. Code available at: https://github.com/polo5/ZeroShotKnowledgeTransfer

papers_seen.author: Yu
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable ones by transferring predictive behavior or internal structure. A range of techniques — from matching teacher soft outputs to aligning intermediate representations, synthesizing or augmenting data, and coordinating multi-teacher or online protocols — enable practical trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and resource constraints. Success depends on task-aware design choices, student capacity, data availability, and careful handling of robustness and social-impact concerns.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Understanding and Improving Lexical Choice in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is essential for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models by reducing the complexity of the raw data with an autoregressive teacher model. In this study, we empirically show that as a side effect of this training, the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words are propagated to the NAT model from the teacher model. To alleviate this problem, we propose to expose the raw data to NAT models to restore the useful information of low-frequency words, which are missed in the distilled data. To this end, we introduce an extra Kullback-Leibler divergence term derived by comparing the lexical choice of NAT model and that embedded in the raw data. Experimental results across language pairs and model architectures demonstrate the effectiveness and universality of the proposed approach. Extensive analyses confirm our claim that our approach improves performance by reducing the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach pushes the SOTA NAT performance on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets up to 27.8 and 33.8 BLEU points, respectively. The source code will be released.

papers_seen.author: Nunez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical but Engineering-Dependent Route to Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of methods for transferring behavior from large teacher models to smaller students, enabling reduced inference cost and deployment on constrained devices. KD can match final outputs or internal representations and is often combined with complementary compression techniques; however, its success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to align architectures, and how to handle data and optimization mismatches. I argue that KD should be treated as an essential, task-aware component of compression pipelines rather than a plug-and-play solution, and I offer practical directions to maximize its benefits while mitigating common failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression strategies enable smaller, faster models to inherit performance from larger teachers by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or ensemble knowledge. Techniques range from logit-based soft-target distillation to feature- and attention-level mimicry, multi-teacher and task-adaptive pipelines, and methods that relax the need for original training data or strong teachers. Across computer vision and natural language processing tasks, distilled students can approach teacher accuracy while drastically reducing parameters and latency; complementary strategies such as careful pre-training of compact models and architecture search further improve trade-offs between efficiency and effectiveness. Key challenges remain in preserving rare-token behavior, aligning heterogeneous teacher–student inputs, and ensuring privacy and robustness during compression.

papers_seen.author: Rice
papers_seen.title: CoReD: Generalizing Fake Media Detection with Continual Representation using Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Over the last few decades, artificial intelligence research has made tremendous strides, but it still heavily relies on fixed datasets in stationary environments. Continual learning is a growing field of research that examines how AI systems can learn sequentially from a continuous stream of linked data in the same way that biological systems do. Simultaneously, fake media such as deepfakes and synthetic face images have emerged as significant to current multimedia technologies. Recently, numerous method has been proposed which can detect deepfakes with high accuracy. However, they suffer significantly due to their reliance on fixed datasets in limited evaluation settings. Therefore, in this work, we apply continuous learning to neural networks' learning dynamics, emphasizing its potential to increase data efficiency significantly. We propose Continual Representation using Distillation (CoReD) method that employs the concept of Continual Learning (CL), Representation Learning (RL), and Knowledge Distillation (KD). We design CoReD to perform sequential domain adaptation tasks on new deepfake and GAN-generated synthetic face datasets, while effectively minimizing the catastrophic forgetting in a teacher-student model setting. Our extensive experimental results demonstrate that our method is efficient at domain adaptation to detect low-quality deepfakes videos and GAN-generated images from several datasets, outperforming the-state-of-art baseline methods.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Graph-less Neural Networks: Teaching Old MLPs New Tricks via Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are popular for graph machine learning and have shown great results on wide node classification tasks. Yet, they are less popular for practical deployments in the industry owing to their scalability challenges incurred by data dependency. Namely, GNN inference depends on neighbor nodes multiple hops away from the target, and fetching them burdens latency-constrained applications. Existing inference acceleration methods like pruning and quantization can speed up GNNs by reducing Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) operations, but the improvements are limited given the data dependency is not resolved. Conversely, multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) have no graph dependency and infer much faster than GNNs, even though they are less accurate than GNNs for node classification in general. Motivated by these complementary strengths and weaknesses, we bring GNNs and MLPs together via knowledge distillation (KD). Our work shows that the performance of MLPs can be improved by large margins with GNN KD. We call the distilled MLPs Graph-less Neural Networks (GLNNs) as they have no inference graph dependency. We show that GLNNs with competitive accuracy infer faster than GNNs by 146X-273X and faster than other acceleration methods by 14X-27X. Under a production setting involving both transductive and inductive predictions across 7 datasets, GLNN accuracies improve over stand-alone MLPs by 12.36% on average and match GNNs on 6/7 datasets. Comprehensive analysis shows when and why GLNNs can achieve competitive accuracies to GNNs and suggests GLNN as a handy choice for latency-constrained applications.

papers_seen.author: Alvarado
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques compress large neural networks into smaller, faster models for practical deployment. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD succeeds through multiple mechanisms — not solely by copying a stronger teacher — enabling many practical variants (logit-based soft targets, feature- and layer-level matching, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free and privacy-preserving protocols). Effective application depends on choosing what and how to transfer, handling data or device constraints, and combining distillation with other compression tools. Key limitations include optimization dynamics, distribution shift for synthetic data, and heterogeneity in federated or privacy-sensitive settings; current research points toward deeper study of representation transfer, optimization effects, and task-aware distillation pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile method for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. It is applied across modalities and deployment constraints and is most effective when combined with complementary compression techniques, careful data and teacher design, and methods that address representation mismatch and optimization. This synthesis summarizes practical techniques, common challenges, and recommended practices for using KD in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers with Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of unifying knowledge from a set of classifiers with different architectures and target classes into a single classifier, given only a generic set of unlabelled data. We call this problem Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers (UHC). This problem is motivated by scenarios where data is collected from multiple sources, but the sources cannot share their data, e.g., due to privacy concerns, and only privately trained models can be shared. In addition, each source may not be able to gather data to train all classes due to data availability at each source, and may not be able to train the same classification model due to different computational resources. To tackle this problem, we propose a generalisation of knowledge distillation to merge HCs. We derive a probabilistic relation between the outputs of HCs and the probability over all classes. Based on this relation, we propose two classes of methods based on cross-entropy minimisation and matrix factorisation, which allow us to estimate soft labels over all classes from unlabelled samples and use them in lieu of ground truth labels to train a unified classifier. Our extensive experiments on ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets show that our approaches significantly outperform a naive extension of distillation and can achieve almost the same accuracy as classifiers that are trained in a centralised, supervised manner.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Trade-offs, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) trains compact student models by transferring information from larger teacher models, enabling deployment under computation, memory, or latency constraints. Across vision, speech, language, and recommendation systems, KD takes many forms — logit matching, feature mimicking, ensemble compression, and data-free synthesis — and is often combined with model pruning, architectural simplification, or curriculum strategies. Effective distillation requires choices about what to transfer (soft targets vs. intermediate features), how to supply or synthesize data, and how to schedule or regularize training; these choices shape outcomes in accuracy, robustness, interpretability, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Bowman
papers_seen.title: TRILLsson: Distilled Universal Paralinguistic Speech Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in self-supervision have dramatically improved the quality of speech representations. However, deployment of state-of-the-art embedding models on devices has been restricted due to their limited public availability and large resource footprint. Our work addresses these issues by publicly releasing a collection of paralinguistic speech models that are small and near state-of-the-art performance. Our approach is based on knowledge distillation, and our models are distilled on public data only. We explore different architectures and thoroughly evaluate our models on the Non-Semantic Speech (NOSS) benchmark. Our largest distilled model is less than 15% the size of the original model (314MB vs 2.2GB), achieves over 96% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks, and is trained on 6.5% the data. The smallest model is 1% in size (22MB) and achieves over 90% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks. Our models outperform the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 model on 6 of 7 tasks, and our smallest model outperforms the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 on both emotion recognition tasks despite being 7% the size.

papers_seen.author: Peterson
papers_seen.title: Understanding Knowledge Distillation in Non-autoregressive Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Non-autoregressive machine translation (NAT) systems predict a sequence of output tokens in parallel, achieving substantial improvements in generation speed compared to autoregressive models. Existing NAT models usually rely on the technique of knowledge distillation, which creates the training data from a pretrained autoregressive model for better performance. Knowledge distillation is empirically useful, leading to large gains in accuracy for NAT models, but the reason for this success has, as of yet, been unclear. In this paper, we first design systematic experiments to investigate why knowledge distillation is crucial to NAT training. We find that knowledge distillation can reduce the complexity of data sets and help NAT to model the variations in the output data. Furthermore, a strong correlation is observed between the capacity of an NAT model and the optimal complexity of the distilled data for the best translation quality. Based on these findings, we further propose several approaches that can alter the complexity of data sets to improve the performance of NAT models. We achieve the state-of-the-art performance for the NAT-based models, and close the gap with the autoregressive baseline on WMT14 En-De benchmark.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Strategy for NLP Model Compression: Promise, Proofs, and Precautions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable approach for compressing large NLP and deep learning models into smaller, deployable students. When combined with complementary techniques—such as architecture-aware compression, data augmentation, and data-free synthesis—KD can deliver much of a teacher model’s performance while greatly reducing inference cost and memory. However, distillation is not without limits: it can propagate teacher biases, depends on careful choice of what and how to transfer, and requires task- and data-aware engineering to be robust in low-data or privacy-sensitive settings. A pragmatic pipeline therefore treats KD as the central tool but couples it with targeted strategies for representation alignment, sample selection, and evaluation under deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: BAM! Born-Again Multi-Task Networks for Natural Language Understanding
papers_seen.abstract: It can be challenging to train multi-task neural networks that outperform or even match their single-task counterparts. To help address this, we propose using knowledge distillation where single-task models teach a multi-task model. We enhance this training with teacher annealing, a novel method that gradually transitions the model from distillation to supervised learning, helping the multi-task model surpass its single-task teachers. We evaluate our approach by multi-task fine-tuning BERT on the GLUE benchmark. Our method consistently improves over standard single-task and multi-task training.

papers_seen.author: Nguyen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical and Multifaceted Tool for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. Across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks, KD enables substantial reductions in memory and inference cost while retaining much of the teacher's performance. However, KD is not a silver bullet: its effectiveness depends on choices of teacher/student architecture, what is distilled (logits, layers, attention, representations), the optimization and data used for distillation, and constraints such as privacy or fairness. Carefully combining KD with techniques like multi-teacher schedules, layer-mapping strategies, task-adaptive compression, and privacy-preserving perturbations yields the best trade-offs for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Lawrence
papers_seen.title: Practical Benefits and Cautions of Knowledge Distillation for NLP Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach to compressing large deep and language models into smaller, faster models suitable for deployment. When applied thoughtfully—using techniques such as data augmentation, multi-teacher training, teacher optimization, or data-free procedures—KD can preserve much of the teacher's utility while reducing inference cost and memory. However, distillation can transfer or amplify undesirable properties of teachers (e.g., biases), and its success depends on choices like which teacher knowledge to transfer and which training samples to use. I argue KD is a powerful tool for NLP model compression but must be combined with targeted strategies for robustness, fairness, privacy, and sample selection to realize its full benefits in practice.

papers_seen.author: Hoffman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Path to Efficient Deep and NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation provides a pragmatic and versatile set of techniques to compress large neural models into compact, faster students while retaining much of their performance. Across NLP and vision, modern distillation variants — including multi-teacher pipelines, self-distillation, teacher optimization, and task-aware layer alignment — address core challenges such as capacity gaps and task-specific redundancy. When combined with complementary compression strategies (pruning, low-precision arithmetic, architecture search), distillation enables deployment of high-performing models under tight resource or latency constraints.

papers_seen.author: Maddox
papers_seen.title: BERT-EMD: Many-to-Many Layer Mapping for BERT Compression with Earth Mover's Distance
papers_seen.abstract: Pre-trained language models (e.g., BERT) have achieved significant success in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, high storage and computational costs obstruct pre-trained language models to be effectively deployed on resource-constrained devices. In this paper, we propose a novel BERT distillation method based on many-to-many layer mapping, which allows each intermediate student layer to learn from any intermediate teacher layers. In this way, our model can learn from different teacher layers adaptively for various NLP tasks. %motivated by the intuition that different NLP tasks require different levels of linguistic knowledge contained in the intermediate layers of BERT. In addition, we leverage Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) to compute the minimum cumulative cost that must be paid to transform knowledge from teacher network to student network. EMD enables the effective matching for many-to-many layer mapping. %EMD can be applied to network layers with different sizes and effectively measures semantic distance between the teacher network and student network. Furthermore, we propose a cost attention mechanism to learn the layer weights used in EMD automatically, which is supposed to further improve the model's performance and accelerate convergence time. Extensive experiments on GLUE benchmark demonstrate that our model achieves competitive performance compared to strong competitors in terms of both accuracy and model compression.

papers_seen.author: Liu
papers_seen.title: Enabling Multimodal Generation on CLIP via Vision-Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The recent large-scale vision-language pre-training (VLP) of dual-stream architectures (e.g., CLIP) with a tremendous amount of image-text pair data, has shown its superiority on various multimodal alignment tasks. Despite its success, the resulting models are not capable of multimodal generative tasks due to the weak text encoder. To tackle this problem, we propose to augment the dual-stream VLP model with a textual pre-trained language model (PLM) via vision-language knowledge distillation (VLKD), enabling the capability for multimodal generation. VLKD is pretty data- and computation-efficient compared to the pre-training from scratch. Experimental results show that the resulting model has strong zero-shot performance on multimodal generation tasks, such as open-ended visual question answering and image captioning. For example, it achieves 44.5% zero-shot accuracy on the VQAv2 dataset, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art zero-shot model with $7\times$ fewer parameters. Furthermore, the original textual language understanding and generation ability of the PLM is maintained after VLKD, which makes our model versatile for both multimodal and unimodal tasks.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a General-Purpose Paradigm: Beyond Compression to Adaptation, Robustness, and Inclusive Deployment
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) began as a technique to compress large models into smaller, faster ones. Over the past decade it has matured into a flexible training paradigm that can shape student behavior via soft targets, intermediate feature alignment, and multi-teacher or self-teaching schemes. When designed with task, data, and deployment constraints in mind, KD can enable domain specialization, interpretability, privacy-friendly federated learning, and improved robustness while still supporting efficient inference.

papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation with Adversarial Samples Supporting Decision Boundary
papers_seen.abstract: Many recent works on knowledge distillation have provided ways to transfer the knowledge of a trained network for improving the learning process of a new one, but finding a good technique for knowledge distillation is still an open problem. In this paper, we provide a new perspective based on a decision boundary, which is one of the most important component of a classifier. The generalization performance of a classifier is closely related to the adequacy of its decision boundary, so a good classifier bears a good decision boundary. Therefore, transferring information closely related to the decision boundary can be a good attempt for knowledge distillation. To realize this goal, we utilize an adversarial attack to discover samples supporting a decision boundary. Based on this idea, to transfer more accurate information about the decision boundary, the proposed algorithm trains a student classifier based on the adversarial samples supporting the decision boundary. Experiments show that the proposed method indeed improves knowledge distillation and achieves the state-of-the-arts performance.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation transfers information from large teacher models to smaller students to reduce inference cost and memory while retaining much of the teacher’s performance. Modern distillation expands beyond matching teacher logits to include intermediate representation matching, self-supervised and contrastive objectives, data-free and synthetic-data schemes, curriculum and augmentation strategies, and privacy- and deployment-aware protocols. These variants enable application across vision, speech, graph-structured data, and NLP, but practical deployment requires care about data availability, optimization dynamics, robustness, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central approach to compress large deep models into smaller, faster, and often more deployable student models. KD techniques range from classic teacher-to-student soft-target training to recent advances including data-free distillation, multi-teacher strategies, meta-learned teachers, and compression combined with pruning or structural sparsity. In NLP applications KD is used to shrink pre-trained transformers, accelerate inference for production systems, enable non-autoregressive generation, and adapt large models to resource-constrained or heterogeneous environments. Empirical work shows KD can preserve much of teacher performance while producing models with far lower latency and storage cost, but theoretical understanding, sensitivity to data and teacher quality, and robustness under distributional shifts remain active research areas.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, production-ready approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, faster ones while retaining much of their performance. KD techniques span teacher design, student-teacher layer mapping, multi-teacher and ensemble strategies, data-aware and data-free workflows, and scalable/online training protocols. When combined with task-aware selection and domain adaptation, distillation enables effective deployment of high-performing models under latency, memory, and heterogeneous-device constraints.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Rejuvenating Low-Frequency Words: Making the Most of Parallel Data in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is commonly used to construct synthetic data for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models. However, there exists a discrepancy on low-frequency words between the distilled and the original data, leading to more errors on predicting low-frequency words. To alleviate the problem, we directly expose the raw data into NAT by leveraging pretraining. By analyzing directed alignments, we found that KD makes low-frequency source words aligned with targets more deterministically but fails to align sufficient low-frequency words from target to source. Accordingly, we propose reverse KD to rejuvenate more alignments for low-frequency target words. To make the most of authentic and synthetic data, we combine these complementary approaches as a new training strategy for further boosting NAT performance. We conduct experiments on five translation benchmarks over two advanced architectures. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly and universally improve translation quality by reducing translation errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach achieves 28.2 and 33.9 BLEU points on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets, respectively. Our code, data, and trained models are available at \url{https://github.com/alphadl/RLFW-NAT}.

papers_seen.author: Hurst
papers_seen.title: Contemporary Approaches and Applications of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger, more costly models to smaller, deployable models. Modern work expands beyond simple soft-label matching to include distillation of internal representations, feature-level imitation, privacy-preserving and data-free strategies, task-adaptive compression, and adaptations to specialized architectures (e.g., GANs, detectors, and transformers). These methods aim to preserve accuracy, robustness, and efficiency (compute, memory, or communication) while enabling deployment on resource-constrained devices or in privacy-sensitive and distributed settings.

papers_seen.author: Decker
papers_seen.title: Practical and Principled Knowledge Distillation for Compressing NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and versatile approach for compressing large deep learning and NLP models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of the teacher’s performance. Effective compression in practice requires matching the distillation technique to the deployment objective: using self-distillation or multi-teacher strategies to extract richer supervisory signals, combining KD with architecture search or pruning for task-specific efficiency, applying appropriate soft/hard label mixing informed by bias–variance tradeoffs, and controlling data and privacy considerations during distillation. When these elements are combined, KD can deliver substantial runtime and memory savings with minimal accuracy loss, making it central to deploying modern NLP systems under resource constraints.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic, widely applicable strategy for producing compact, deployable models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. KD works across modalities and deployment constraints, and supports extensions for data-free, federated, and privacy-sensitive settings. However, realizing KD’s full potential requires careful choices about what signals to transfer (logits, features, relational signals), how to align teacher and student architectures, and how to mitigate transferred harms such as bias or degraded rare-token behavior. When combined with complementary methods (augmentation, layer-aware mapping, multi-teacher ensembles, or differential-privacy mechanisms), KD becomes a flexible core of effective compression pipelines for real-world NLP and deep-learning systems.

papers_seen.author: Bright
papers_seen.title: Towards Practical Lipreading with Distilled and Efficient Models
papers_seen.abstract: Lipreading has witnessed a lot of progress due to the resurgence of neural networks. Recent works have placed emphasis on aspects such as improving performance by finding the optimal architecture or improving generalization. However, there is still a significant gap between the current methodologies and the requirements for an effective deployment of lipreading in practical scenarios. In this work, we propose a series of innovations that significantly bridge that gap: first, we raise the state-of-the-art performance by a wide margin on LRW and LRW-1000 to 88.5% and 46.6%, respectively using self-distillation. Secondly, we propose a series of architectural changes, including a novel Depthwise Separable Temporal Convolutional Network (DS-TCN) head, that slashes the computational cost to a fraction of the (already quite efficient) original model. Thirdly, we show that knowledge distillation is a very effective tool for recovering performance of the lightweight models. This results in a range of models with different accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. However, our most promising lightweight models are on par with the current state-of-the-art while showing a reduction of 8.2x and 3.9x in terms of computational cost and number of parameters, respectively, which we hope will enable the deployment of lipreading models in practical applications.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller student models to reduce compute, memory, and latency while preserving task performance. Across vision, speech, and language tasks, KD has been adapted into many forms—soft-target matching, intermediate representation alignment, attention and relational transfers, multi-teacher ensembles, online distillation, and task-adaptive pipelines—and combined with orthogonal compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to enable deployment in resource-constrained or privacy-sensitive settings. Empirical work shows KD often recovers most of a teacher's utility in a much smaller footprint, but success depends on teacher quality, the choice of distilled signals, data availability and domain shift, and robustness and privacy constraints. The field continues to refine objectives, layer-mapping strategies, and workflows that make distillation effective across modalities and large pretrained models in practical deployments.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applied strategy to transfer information from large or specialized teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. In practice KD has been used to compress pretrained language models, speed up inference in structured models, enable multimodal generation, improve low-precision networks, and scale training across data-parallel workers. Research spans theoretical analyses of why distillation works, empirical studies of failure modes (e.g., propagation of teacher errors), and practical training recipes (including online and self-distillation variants) that balance fidelity to the teacher with student capacity and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Cameron
papers_seen.title: Well-Read Students Learn Better: On the Importance of Pre-training Compact Models
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in natural language representations have been accompanied by large and expensive models that leverage vast amounts of general-domain text through self-supervised pre-training. Due to the cost of applying such models to down-stream tasks, several model compression techniques on pre-trained language representations have been proposed (Sun et al., 2019; Sanh, 2019). However, surprisingly, the simple baseline of just pre-training and fine-tuning compact models has been overlooked. In this paper, we first show that pre-training remains important in the context of smaller architectures, and fine-tuning pre-trained compact models can be competitive to more elaborate methods proposed in concurrent work. Starting with pre-trained compact models, we then explore transferring task knowledge from large fine-tuned models through standard knowledge distillation. The resulting simple, yet effective and general algorithm, Pre-trained Distillation, brings further improvements. Through extensive experiments, we more generally explore the interaction between pre-training and distillation under two variables that have been under-studied: model size and properties of unlabeled task data. One surprising observation is that they have a compound effect even when sequentially applied on the same data. To accelerate future research, we will make our 24 pre-trained miniature BERT models publicly available.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Highlight Every Step: Knowledge Distillation via Collaborative Teaching
papers_seen.abstract: High storage and computational costs obstruct deep neural networks to be deployed on resource-constrained devices. Knowledge distillation aims to train a compact student network by transferring knowledge from a larger pre-trained teacher model. However, most existing methods on knowledge distillation ignore the valuable information among training process associated with training results. In this paper, we provide a new Collaborative Teaching Knowledge Distillation (CTKD) strategy which employs two special teachers. Specifically, one teacher trained from scratch (i.e., scratch teacher) assists the student step by step using its temporary outputs. It forces the student to approach the optimal path towards the final logits with high accuracy. The other pre-trained teacher (i.e., expert teacher) guides the student to focus on a critical region which is more useful for the task. The combination of the knowledge from two special teachers can significantly improve the performance of the student network in knowledge distillation. The results of experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN and Tiny ImageNet datasets verify that the proposed knowledge distillation method is efficient and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

papers_seen.author: Davidson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad family of techniques that transfer knowledge from larger, more expensive models (teachers) into smaller, efficient models (students) to improve inference speed, reduce memory, or enable deployment in resource-constrained settings. Across vision, language, graph, and generative modeling, KD has been instantiated as matching soft outputs, aligning internal representations, or supervising task-specific components. Practical work has shown KD can produce compact models with strong empirical performance, but success depends on many factors including student capacity, the choice of distilled signals, availability of data, training efficiency, and privacy constraints. Recent research has focused on richer teacher-to-student signals (intermediate layers, attention-based fusion), teacher adaptation strategies, data and augmentation strategies for better transfer, and integrating KD with pruning and other compression methods. Important open issues remain around optimization limits, data heterogeneity, and privacy-preserving distillation protocols.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical but Design-Sensitive Path to Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly useful family of techniques for transferring behavior from large teacher models to smaller students to reduce inference cost and enable deployment. KD has been instantiated as matching soft targets, aligning intermediate representations, progressive module replacement, and selective or multi-teacher schemes. While KD often yields strong empirical gains and enables domain- and task-specific compression, its success depends on optimization dynamics, the choice of distilled signal, data quality and selection, and teacher–student alignment. Careful method choices make KD a reliable, production-ready compression strategy, but it is not a universal shortcut: practitioners must tailor KD objectives and protocols to their constraints and goals.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: On Representation Knowledge Distillation for Graph Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a learning paradigm for boosting resource-efficient graph neural networks (GNNs) using more expressive yet cumbersome teacher models. Past work on distillation for GNNs proposed the Local Structure Preserving loss (LSP), which matches local structural relationships defined over edges across the student and teacher's node embeddings. This paper studies whether preserving the global topology of how the teacher embeds graph data can be a more effective distillation objective for GNNs, as real-world graphs often contain latent interactions and noisy edges. We propose Graph Contrastive Representation Distillation (G-CRD), which uses contrastive learning to implicitly preserve global topology by aligning the student node embeddings to those of the teacher in a shared representation space. Additionally, we introduce an expanded set of benchmarks on large-scale real-world datasets where the performance gap between teacher and student GNNs is non-negligible. Experiments across 4 datasets and 14 heterogeneous GNN architectures show that G-CRD consistently boosts the performance and robustness of lightweight GNNs, outperforming LSP (and a global structure preserving variant of LSP) as well as baselines from 2D computer vision. An analysis of the representational similarity among teacher and student embedding spaces reveals that G-CRD balances preserving local and global relationships, while structure preserving approaches are best at preserving one or the other. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Efficient and Responsible NLP and Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical, versatile approach for compressing large models and enabling deployment in resource-constrained environments. Beyond raw compression, KD supports domain adaptation, data-free scenarios, improved inference speed, and novel training regimes for specialized tasks. However, distillation is not a panacea: it can amplify teacher biases, interact with regularization techniques in subtle ways, and benefits most when combined with complementary methods such as architecture-aware training, generator-based sample synthesis, or instance-aware losses.

papers_seen.author: Zuniga
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Composable Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and practical technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable student models. KD is effective across modalities (vision, speech, language, graphs) and settings (task-specific compression, data-limited or data-free transfer), and its strengths are amplified when combined with complementary methods such as architecture-aware replacement, pruning, low-precision numerics, adaptive teacher design, and careful input-side practices. To realize robust and fair compressed models, practitioners should treat KD as one tool within a pipeline: design student-friendly teachers, account for data constraints, use augmentation and curriculum where helpful, and combine KD with orthogonal compression techniques.

papers_seen.author: Richards
papers_seen.title: TextKD-GAN: Text Generation using KnowledgeDistillation and Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Text generation is of particular interest in many NLP applications such as machine translation, language modeling, and text summarization. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) achieved a remarkable success in high quality image generation in computer vision,and recently, GANs have gained lots of interest from the NLP community as well. However, achieving similar success in NLP would be more challenging due to the discrete nature of text. In this work, we introduce a method using knowledge distillation to effectively exploit GAN setup for text generation. We demonstrate how autoencoders (AEs) can be used for providing a continuous representation of sentences, which is a smooth representation that assign non-zero probabilities to more than one word. We distill this representation to train the generator to synthesize similar smooth representations. We perform a number of experiments to validate our idea using different datasets and show that our proposed approach yields better performance in terms of the BLEU score and Jensen-Shannon distance (JSD) measure compared to traditional GAN-based text generation approaches without pre-training.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: A Deep Hierarchical Approach to Lifelong Learning in Minecraft
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a lifelong learning system that has the ability to reuse and transfer knowledge from one task to another while efficiently retaining the previously learned knowledge-base. Knowledge is transferred by learning reusable skills to solve tasks in Minecraft, a popular video game which is an unsolved and high-dimensional lifelong learning problem. These reusable skills, which we refer to as Deep Skill Networks, are then incorporated into our novel Hierarchical Deep Reinforcement Learning Network (H-DRLN) architecture using two techniques: (1) a deep skill array and (2) skill distillation, our novel variation of policy distillation (Rusu et. al. 2015) for learning skills. Skill distillation enables the HDRLN to efficiently retain knowledge and therefore scale in lifelong learning, by accumulating knowledge and encapsulating multiple reusable skills into a single distilled network. The H-DRLN exhibits superior performance and lower learning sample complexity compared to the regular Deep Q Network (Mnih et. al. 2015) in sub-domains of Minecraft.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a broadly applicable toolkit for transferring capability from large, expensive teacher models to smaller, faster, or more privacy-friendly student models. Methods range from transferring softened output distributions to aligning intermediate representations, using synthetic or augmented data when original data are unavailable, and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). KD is used both as a deployment-oriented compression strategy and as a general training paradigm that can improve regularization, robustness, and domain adaptation. Practical success requires careful matching of distillation objectives, teacher-student alignment, and data strategies; persistent challenges include theoretical understanding of when distillation helps, preserving rare-token behavior in NLP, and avoiding artifacts introduced by synthetic data.

papers_seen.author: Heath
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and flexible approach for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers across vision, language, speech, and multimodal settings. Methods range from matching teacher logits to aligning intermediate representations, ensembling or self-teaching, and combining distillation with pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Empirical work shows KD can preserve much of a teacher's performance while enabling deployment under compute, memory, privacy, and latency constraints, but effectiveness depends on choices of distilled signals, data and augmentations, teacher–student alignment, and task-aware pipeline design.
