papers_seen.author: Kim
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When paired with representation-aware objectives, careful pre-training of compact models, and safeguards for robustness and privacy, KD enables production-ready reductions in latency, memory, and energy while retaining much of a teacher's performance. I argue that KD should be treated as a central tool in model-compression pipelines, not as a single recipe but as a family of methods to be combined with task-aware design choices for reliable deployment.

papers_seen.author: Wagner
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation in Natural Language Processing
papers_seen.abstract: Since deep learning became a key player in natural language processing (NLP), many deep learning models have been showing remarkable performances in a variety of NLP tasks, and in some cases, they are even outperforming humans. Such high performance can be explained by efficient knowledge representation of deep learning models. While many methods have been proposed to learn more efficient representation, knowledge distillation from pretrained deep networks suggest that we can use more information from the soft target probability to train other neural networks. In this paper, we propose a new knowledge distillation method self-knowledge distillation, based on the soft target probabilities of the training model itself, where multimode information is distilled from the word embedding space right below the softmax layer. Due to the time complexity, our method approximates the soft target probabilities. In experiments, we applied the proposed method to two different and fundamental NLP tasks: language model and neural machine translation. The experiment results show that our proposed method improves performance on the tasks.

papers_seen.author: Roman
papers_seen.title: Fair Feature Distillation for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Fairness is becoming an increasingly crucial issue for computer vision, especially in the human-related decision systems. However, achieving algorithmic fairness, which makes a model produce indiscriminative outcomes against protected groups, is still an unresolved problem. In this paper, we devise a systematic approach which reduces algorithmic biases via feature distillation for visual recognition tasks, dubbed as MMD-based Fair Distillation (MFD). While the distillation technique has been widely used in general to improve the prediction accuracy, to the best of our knowledge, there has been no explicit work that also tries to improve fairness via distillation. Furthermore, We give a theoretical justification of our MFD on the effect of knowledge distillation and fairness. Throughout the extensive experiments, we show our MFD significantly mitigates the bias against specific minorities without any loss of the accuracy on both synthetic and real-world face datasets.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Understanding BERT Rankers Under Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep language models such as BERT pre-trained on large corpus have given a huge performance boost to the state-of-the-art information retrieval ranking systems. Knowledge embedded in such models allows them to pick up complex matching signals between passages and queries. However, the high computation cost during inference limits their deployment in real-world search scenarios. In this paper, we study if and how the knowledge for search within BERT can be transferred to a smaller ranker through distillation. Our experiments demonstrate that it is crucial to use a proper distillation procedure, which produces up to nine times speedup while preserving the state-of-the-art performance.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, broadly applicable approach to compressing large models for deployment in resource-constrained settings. KD enables model-size and compute reductions while preserving task performance, and it integrates naturally with other compression techniques, privacy-preserving releases, federated and heterogeneous-device training, and domain/continual adaptation. However, its success depends on careful choices: how teacher signals are generated and weighted, which data (or synthetic/meta-data) drive distillation, and how KD interacts with data heterogeneity and fairness constraints. When combined with complementary methods (pruning, architecture search, data augmentation, selective sample weighting), KD yields efficient models that retain much of the teacher’s capabilities across vision, generative, and language tasks.

papers_seen.author: Riley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is not merely a model-compression trick but a central, practical paradigm for deploying high-performance deep and NLP models under real-world constraints. KD can compress large pre-trained models into lightweight students, transfer inductive biases, improve robustness and generalization, enable low-precision and privacy-aware deployments, and adapt to data- or compute-limited settings. Effective distillation couples soft-label transfer with representation-level alignment, task-aware architecture choices, and complementary techniques (quantization, pruning, augmentation). However, KD must be applied carefully: teacher–student mismatches, bias transfer, domain shift, and limited-data regimes require method choices such as feature mimicking, teacher ensembles, teacher-free objectives, or fairness-aware augmentations. The result is a flexible toolkit that—when combined with architectural and data strategies—makes high-quality, efficient models feasible for production NLP and deep-learning systems.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses or transfers knowledge from larger or multiple models into smaller, faster models by leveraging softer training signals, intermediate representations, or alternate training protocols. Research has explored KD’s theoretical underpinnings, practical training strategies (including teacher-ensemble and teacher-free variants), privacy- and communication-aware settings, and extensions beyond classification to generation and structured prediction. Empirical work demonstrates KD’s ability to reduce deployment cost while retaining or sometimes even improving downstream performance, but trade-offs remain around data availability, representation matching, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: BERT-of-Theseus: Compressing BERT by Progressive Module Replacing
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel model compression approach to effectively compress BERT by progressive module replacing. Our approach first divides the original BERT into several modules and builds their compact substitutes. Then, we randomly replace the original modules with their substitutes to train the compact modules to mimic the behavior of the original modules. We progressively increase the probability of replacement through the training. In this way, our approach brings a deeper level of interaction between the original and compact models. Compared to the previous knowledge distillation approaches for BERT compression, our approach does not introduce any additional loss function. Our approach outperforms existing knowledge distillation approaches on GLUE benchmark, showing a new perspective of model compression.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Unifying Paradigm for Compression, Adaptation, and Robust Training
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be considered not merely as a compression trick but as a general and practical training paradigm. Across modalities and tasks, KD transfers information about function, structure, and uncertainty from one model (or ensemble) to another, enabling smaller, faster, or more adaptable models while improving generalization, interpretability, and domain transfer. Success depends on how teacher knowledge is selected, represented, and combined with data-side techniques; thoughtful design choices (layer mapping, sample selection, augmentation, and teacher trust) determine whether KD yields compression, robustness, or better task-specific performance.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques provide practical routes to deploy large, high-performance neural models in resource- constrained or latency-sensitive settings. Methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, relational structure), how training data is used or synthesized, and whether compression is task-agnostic or task-adaptive. In natural language tasks, KD has enabled dramatic size and speed gains for large pretrained models (e.g., BERT) as well as the feasibility of simple architectures that retain most of the original performance. Despite empirical success, challenges remain: choosing what to transfer for maximal utility, constructing or selecting suitable training examples, handling heterogeneous or private data (federated or data-free settings), and designing teacher-student curricula or architectures that improve transfer. Emerging directions include task-adaptive compression, many-to-many layer alignment, multi-teacher and teacher-aware training, and principled approaches to data selection or generation during distillation.

papers_seen.author: Mahoney
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Context-Sensitive Path to Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible technique for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact student models. When combined with feature-level objectives, architectural transformations, teacher optimization, and data strategies, KD can recover much of a teacher's performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, its success depends on task and domain specifics, teacher quality, student capacity, and data availability; therefore, practitioners should treat KD as a toolbox to be adapted—not a single recipe—to obtain reliable compression in real-world systems.

papers_seen.author: Walton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential, Practical Strategy for Compressing Deep Models in NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques are indispensable for deploying high-capacity deep and language models in resource-constrained settings. By transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teachers to smaller students, practitioners can achieve large reductions in model size and latency while retaining most task performance. However, realizing these gains reliably requires attention to what is transferred (logits, features, relations), how teachers and data are chosen, and hardware- or deployment-aware compression strategies.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Moonshine: Distilling with Cheap Convolutions
papers_seen.abstract: Many engineers wish to deploy modern neural networks in memory-limited settings; but the development of flexible methods for reducing memory use is in its infancy, and there is little knowledge of the resulting cost-benefit. We propose structural model distillation for memory reduction using a strategy that produces a student architecture that is a simple transformation of the teacher architecture: no redesign is needed, and the same hyperparameters can be used. Using attention transfer, we provide Pareto curves/tables for distillation of residual networks with four benchmark datasets, indicating the memory versus accuracy payoff. We show that substantial memory savings are possible with very little loss of accuracy, and confirm that distillation provides student network performance that is better than training that student architecture directly on data.

papers_seen.author: Maddox
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Tool for Compression, Bias Transfer, and Robust Deployment
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is more than a model compression trick: it is a practical mechanism for transferring inductive biases, regularizing students, enabling privacy- and data-constrained deployments, and adapting architectures or modalities. When paired with complementary techniques—data augmentation, curriculum schedules, teacher ensembles, or generative replay—KD consistently narrows the gap between compact students and large teachers while addressing real-world constraints such as limited labeled data, compute, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Rios
papers_seen.title: Improving Neural Topic Models using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Topic models are often used to identify human-interpretable topics to help make sense of large document collections. We use knowledge distillation to combine the best attributes of probabilistic topic models and pretrained transformers. Our modular method can be straightforwardly applied with any neural topic model to improve topic quality, which we demonstrate using two models having disparate architectures, obtaining state-of-the-art topic coherence. We show that our adaptable framework not only improves performance in the aggregate over all estimated topics, as is commonly reported, but also in head-to-head comparisons of aligned topics.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Flexible Path to Compact and Robust NLP and Deep Learning Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and versatile set of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster ones while retaining most of their performance. Distillation methods can be adapted to structural compression, domain adaptation, low-data or no-data scenarios, and different model families (transformers, convolutional nets, graph models). A pragmatic compression strategy combines well-chosen distillation objectives with complementary methods (pruning, architecture transformations, multi-teacher supervision, or data-generation) to meet deployment constraints without sacrificing reliability.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Improved Feature Distillation via Projector Ensemble
papers_seen.abstract: In knowledge distillation, previous feature distillation methods mainly focus on the design of loss functions and the selection of the distilled layers, while the effect of the feature projector between the student and the teacher remains under-explored. In this paper, we first discuss a plausible mechanism of the projector with empirical evidence and then propose a new feature distillation method based on a projector ensemble for further performance improvement. We observe that the student network benefits from a projector even if the feature dimensions of the student and the teacher are the same. Training a student backbone without a projector can be considered as a multi-task learning process, namely achieving discriminative feature extraction for classification and feature matching between the student and the teacher for distillation at the same time. We hypothesize and empirically verify that without a projector, the student network tends to overfit the teacher's feature distributions despite having different architecture and weights initialization. This leads to degradation on the quality of the student's deep features that are eventually used in classification. Adding a projector, on the other hand, disentangles the two learning tasks and helps the student network to focus better on the main feature extraction task while still being able to utilize teacher features as a guidance through the projector. Motivated by the positive effect of the projector in feature distillation, we propose an ensemble of projectors to further improve the quality of student features. Experimental results on different datasets with a series of teacher-student pairs illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

papers_seen.author: Allison
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a core strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable ones by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from teacher models to students. The field has diversified from logits-only matching to richer targets (intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals), multiple training regimes (data-free, online, federated, multi-teacher), and task-aware techniques that address capacity mismatch and deployment constraints. KD is widely applicable across modalities (vision, speech, multimodal, graphs, NLP) and is most effective when combined with data- and architecture-aware practices, but practical limits remain around representation alignment, rare-token behavior, privacy, and domain transfer.

papers_seen.author: Welch
papers_seen.title: Distillation as Default: A Practical Position on Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a necessary and practical core technique for compressing large deep models into deployable, efficient students. When combined with representation-level matching, careful pre-training of compact students, and attention to privacy and deployment constraints, KD preserves much of teacher performance while enabling low-latency, on-device, and federated use. However, naive soft-label matching is insufficient: best practice integrates intermediate-feature supervision, data- and architecture-aware pipelines, and multi-stage or multi-teacher strategies to handle domain shift, rare phenomena, and heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Cohen
papers_seen.title: ALP-KD: Attention-Based Layer Projection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is considered as a training and compression strategy in which two neural networks, namely a teacher and a student, are coupled together during training. The teacher network is supposed to be a trustworthy predictor and the student tries to mimic its predictions. Usually, a student with a lighter architecture is selected so we can achieve compression and yet deliver high-quality results. In such a setting, distillation only happens for final predictions whereas the student could also benefit from teacher's supervision for internal components.   Motivated by this, we studied the problem of distillation for intermediate layers. Since there might not be a one-to-one alignment between student and teacher layers, existing techniques skip some teacher layers and only distill from a subset of them. This shortcoming directly impacts quality, so we instead propose a combinatorial technique which relies on attention. Our model fuses teacher-side information and takes each layer's significance into consideration, then performs distillation between combined teacher layers and those of the student. Using our technique, we distilled a 12-layer BERT (Devlin et al. 2019) into 6-, 4-, and 2-layer counterparts and evaluated them on GLUE tasks (Wang et al. 2018). Experimental results show that our combinatorial approach is able to outperform other existing techniques.

papers_seen.author: Mueller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central, pragmatic approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. KD delivers strong empirical gains across domains by transferring soft outputs, intermediate representations, or task-specific behaviors from teachers to students. Its strengths are practical: it supports deployment on constrained hardware, enables multi-teacher and cross-model transfer, and integrates with other compression tools. At the same time, KD is not a plug-and-play solution: theoretical and empirical work shows limits under data heterogeneity, imperfect teachers, and mismatched architectures, so KD must be applied with task-aware choices (signal type, layer alignment, teacher selection, and curricula) and often combined with complementary methods to realize reliable, high-fidelity compression.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation transfers information from large teacher models to smaller students to reduce inference cost and memory while retaining much of the teacher’s performance. Modern distillation expands beyond matching teacher logits to include intermediate representation matching, self-supervised and contrastive objectives, data-free and synthetic-data schemes, curriculum and augmentation strategies, and privacy- and deployment-aware protocols. These variants enable application across vision, speech, graph-structured data, and NLP, but practical deployment requires care about data availability, optimization dynamics, robustness, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models by transferring information from a high-capacity teacher to a smaller student so the student retains much of the teacher’s predictive power while using less compute, memory, or latency. The literature has expanded KD beyond matching teacher soft-labels to include intermediate-feature and layer-wise matching, online/self-distillation, data-free and privacy-aware methods, and combinations with architectural compression (pruning, quantization, and architecture search). Empirical results across vision, NLP, speech, graphs, and ranking show that distilled students often recover a large fraction of teacher performance, but practical success depends on choices like teacher design, student capacity, layer alignment, data availability, and training schedules. Remaining challenges include handling low-frequency or fine-grained behaviors, optimization and capacity mismatch, matching heterogeneous architectures, and distilling under privacy or data-scarce constraints.

papers_seen.author: Aguirre
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques transfer information from large, high-capacity teacher models to smaller student models to reduce model size, latency, and deployment cost while retaining much of the teacher's utility. Methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, ensembles), how training data is used or synthesized, and whether distillation is combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Across vision and NLP tasks, distillation enables practical deployment of compact models but requires careful handling of representation mismatch, data availability, optimization schedules, and potential amplification of teacher errors or biases.

papers_seen.author: Wagner
papers_seen.title: Survey of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, faster students by transferring information from a teacher. Techniques extend beyond using teacher soft outputs (soft labels) to include internal representation matching, layer alignment, task-aware selection of teacher information, data-free synthesis, online mutual teaching, and architecture search guided by distillation. Practical work on NLP (especially BERT-family models), generative models, and domain- or modality-specific settings demonstrates that combining pre-training, architecture-aware search, and representation-level distillation often yields the best trade-offs between efficiency and downstream performance. Open challenges remain around imperfect teachers, optimization and capacity mismatch, data availability, and robustness/generalization under distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large models by transferring useful information from one or more teacher models to a smaller student model, enabling faster inference, lower memory use, and domain- or deployment-specific adaptation. Research has developed multiple distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals), teacher-management strategies (ensembles, multi-teacher weighting, teacher-training), data strategies (data-aware curricula, data-free synthesis), and complementary techniques (projector layers, adversarial objectives, curriculum schedules). Empirical work shows that careful selection of what to transfer and how to align teacher and student—balanced with attention to optimization dynamics and data constraints—produces compact models that preserve much of the teacher’s performance while meeting real-world latency, privacy, and robustness requirements.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Trade-offs, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) trains compact student models by transferring information from larger teacher models, enabling deployment under computation, memory, or latency constraints. Across vision, speech, language, and recommendation systems, KD takes many forms — logit matching, feature mimicking, ensemble compression, and data-free synthesis — and is often combined with model pruning, architectural simplification, or curriculum strategies. Effective distillation requires choices about what to transfer (soft targets vs. intermediate features), how to supply or synthesize data, and how to schedule or regularize training; these choices shape outcomes in accuracy, robustness, interpretability, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Novak
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression methods enable transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large, high-capacity teachers to smaller students so models can be deployed under computation, memory, latency, or privacy constraints. The literature shows a spectrum of approaches — from matching softened output distributions to feature- and layer-level imitation, attention-guided alignment, data-free or zero-shot synthesis of training examples, and distributed or privacy-aware protocols — and demonstrates successful applications across vision, speech, recommendation, and many NLP tasks. Practical effectiveness depends on choices of distillation signal, data availability and synthesis, teacher–student architecture alignment, and training curricula; open challenges include handling imperfect teachers, preserving rare or long-tail behaviors, and maintaining robustness under distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Cameron
papers_seen.title: Well-Read Students Learn Better: On the Importance of Pre-training Compact Models
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in natural language representations have been accompanied by large and expensive models that leverage vast amounts of general-domain text through self-supervised pre-training. Due to the cost of applying such models to down-stream tasks, several model compression techniques on pre-trained language representations have been proposed (Sun et al., 2019; Sanh, 2019). However, surprisingly, the simple baseline of just pre-training and fine-tuning compact models has been overlooked. In this paper, we first show that pre-training remains important in the context of smaller architectures, and fine-tuning pre-trained compact models can be competitive to more elaborate methods proposed in concurrent work. Starting with pre-trained compact models, we then explore transferring task knowledge from large fine-tuned models through standard knowledge distillation. The resulting simple, yet effective and general algorithm, Pre-trained Distillation, brings further improvements. Through extensive experiments, we more generally explore the interaction between pre-training and distillation under two variables that have been under-studied: model size and properties of unlabeled task data. One surprising observation is that they have a compound effect even when sequentially applied on the same data. To accelerate future research, we will make our 24 pre-trained miniature BERT models publicly available.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Compressing and Adapting NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a principled way to produce small, fast models that retain much of the performance of larger networks. In natural language processing, where modern pretrained models are large and domain shifts are common, KD enables domain adaptation, latency- and memory-constrained deployment, continual learning, and improved robustness when applied with the right strategies. Practical success relies on combining methods — e.g., multi-stage distillation, selective or curriculum-driven example selection, leveraging soft targets as regularizers, and using adversarial or synthetic data when original data are unavailable. When applied thoughtfully, KD is not merely an implementation detail of model compression but a versatile lever for engineering efficient, accurate, and robust NLP systems.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Flexible Path to Compact and Robust NLP and Deep Learning Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and versatile set of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster ones while retaining most of their performance. Distillation methods can be adapted to structural compression, domain adaptation, low-data or no-data scenarios, and different model families (transformers, convolutional nets, graph models). A pragmatic compression strategy combines well-chosen distillation objectives with complementary methods (pruning, architecture transformations, multi-teacher supervision, or data-generation) to meet deployment constraints without sacrificing reliability.

papers_seen.author: Harrell
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques have become central tools to deploy high-capacity deep models in latency-, memory-, privacy-, and compute-constrained settings. Across vision, language, graph, and multimodal domains, practitioners use teacher-student training, feature-level transfer, data-free distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine pruning or architecture search with distillation. Work in this area balances fidelity to teacher models, robustness, and efficiency, and explores trade-offs such as reliance on original training data, communication overhead in federated settings, and the benefits of designing students or student-friendly teachers. The literature shows repeated success of KD when tailored to the task and constraints, while also revealing limitations under severe data heterogeneity or adversarial settings.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: SEED: Self-supervised Distillation For Visual Representation
papers_seen.abstract: This paper is concerned with self-supervised learning for small models. The problem is motivated by our empirical studies that while the widely used contrastive self-supervised learning method has shown great progress on large model training, it does not work well for small models. To address this problem, we propose a new learning paradigm, named SElf-SupErvised Distillation (SEED), where we leverage a larger network (as Teacher) to transfer its representational knowledge into a smaller architecture (as Student) in a self-supervised fashion. Instead of directly learning from unlabeled data, we train a student encoder to mimic the similarity score distribution inferred by a teacher over a set of instances. We show that SEED dramatically boosts the performance of small networks on downstream tasks. Compared with self-supervised baselines, SEED improves the top-1 accuracy from 42.2% to 67.6% on EfficientNet-B0 and from 36.3% to 68.2% on MobileNet-v3-Large on the ImageNet-1k dataset.

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Few Shot Network Compression via Cross Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Model compression has been widely adopted to obtain light-weighted deep neural networks. Most prevalent methods, however, require fine-tuning with sufficient training data to ensure accuracy, which could be challenged by privacy and security issues. As a compromise between privacy and performance, in this paper we investigate few shot network compression: given few samples per class, how can we effectively compress the network with negligible performance drop? The core challenge of few shot network compression lies in high estimation errors from the original network during inference, since the compressed network can easily over-fits on the few training instances. The estimation errors could propagate and accumulate layer-wisely and finally deteriorate the network output. To address the problem, we propose cross distillation, a novel layer-wise knowledge distillation approach. By interweaving hidden layers of teacher and student network, layer-wisely accumulated estimation errors can be effectively reduced.The proposed method offers a general framework compatible with prevalent network compression techniques such as pruning. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that cross distillation can significantly improve the student network's accuracy when only a few training instances are available.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Online Knowledge Distillation via Mutual Contrastive Learning for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: The teacher-free online Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to train an ensemble of multiple student models collaboratively and distill knowledge from each other. Although existing online KD methods achieve desirable performance, they often focus on class probabilities as the core knowledge type, ignoring the valuable feature representational information. We present a Mutual Contrastive Learning (MCL) framework for online KD. The core idea of MCL is to perform mutual interaction and transfer of contrastive distributions among a cohort of networks in an online manner. Our MCL can aggregate cross-network embedding information and maximize the lower bound to the mutual information between two networks. This enables each network to learn extra contrastive knowledge from others, leading to better feature representations, thus improving the performance of visual recognition tasks. Beyond the final layer, we extend MCL to intermediate layers and perform an adaptive layer-matching mechanism trained by meta-optimization. Experiments on image classification and transfer learning to visual recognition tasks show that layer-wise MCL can lead to consistent performance gains against state-of-the-art online KD approaches. The superiority demonstrates that layer-wise MCL can guide the network to generate better feature representations. Our code is publicly avaliable at https://github.com/winycg/L-MCL.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Graph-less Neural Networks: Teaching Old MLPs New Tricks via Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are popular for graph machine learning and have shown great results on wide node classification tasks. Yet, they are less popular for practical deployments in the industry owing to their scalability challenges incurred by data dependency. Namely, GNN inference depends on neighbor nodes multiple hops away from the target, and fetching them burdens latency-constrained applications. Existing inference acceleration methods like pruning and quantization can speed up GNNs by reducing Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) operations, but the improvements are limited given the data dependency is not resolved. Conversely, multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) have no graph dependency and infer much faster than GNNs, even though they are less accurate than GNNs for node classification in general. Motivated by these complementary strengths and weaknesses, we bring GNNs and MLPs together via knowledge distillation (KD). Our work shows that the performance of MLPs can be improved by large margins with GNN KD. We call the distilled MLPs Graph-less Neural Networks (GLNNs) as they have no inference graph dependency. We show that GLNNs with competitive accuracy infer faster than GNNs by 146X-273X and faster than other acceleration methods by 14X-27X. Under a production setting involving both transductive and inductive predictions across 7 datasets, GLNN accuracies improve over stand-alone MLPs by 12.36% on average and match GNNs on 6/7 datasets. Comprehensive analysis shows when and why GLNNs can achieve competitive accuracies to GNNs and suggests GLNN as a handy choice for latency-constrained applications.

papers_seen.author: Harrell
papers_seen.title: No One Left Behind: Inclusive Federated Learning over Heterogeneous Devices
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is an important paradigm for training global models from decentralized data in a privacy-preserving way. Existing FL methods usually assume the global model can be trained on any participating client. However, in real applications, the devices of clients are usually heterogeneous, and have different computing power. Although big models like BERT have achieved huge success in AI, it is difficult to apply them to heterogeneous FL with weak clients. The straightforward solutions like removing the weak clients or using a small model to fit all clients will lead to some problems, such as under-representation of dropped clients and inferior accuracy due to data loss or limited model representation ability. In this work, we propose InclusiveFL, a client-inclusive federated learning method to handle this problem. The core idea of InclusiveFL is to assign models of different sizes to clients with different computing capabilities, bigger models for powerful clients and smaller ones for weak clients. We also propose an effective method to share the knowledge among multiple local models with different sizes. In this way, all the clients can participate in the model learning in FL, and the final model can be big and powerful enough. Besides, we propose a momentum knowledge distillation method to better transfer knowledge in big models on powerful clients to the small models on weak clients. Extensive experiments on many real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in learning accurate models from clients with heterogeneous devices under the FL framework.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Beyond Soft Labels: A Practical Position on Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a crucial technique for shrinking large deep models to meet real-world latency, memory and privacy constraints while retaining much of their performance. However, naive distillation that only matches teacher soft-labels is often insufficient. A more reliable strategy combines distillation of internal representations and features, task- or domain-adaptive compression, and architecture-aware search or adaptation. When applied with care — addressing optimization issues, data or privacy limits, and mismatch between teacher and student capacities — distillation enables compact, fast models that approach teacher performance across speech, NLP and vision tasks.

papers_seen.author: Nguyen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical and Multifaceted Tool for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. Across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks, KD enables substantial reductions in memory and inference cost while retaining much of the teacher's performance. However, KD is not a silver bullet: its effectiveness depends on choices of teacher/student architecture, what is distilled (logits, layers, attention, representations), the optimization and data used for distillation, and constraints such as privacy or fairness. Carefully combining KD with techniques like multi-teacher schedules, layer-mapping strategies, task-adaptive compression, and privacy-preserving perturbations yields the best trade-offs for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Chavez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Compression: Effective but Context-Sensitive
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and practical approach to compress large neural models into smaller, faster, or more hardware-friendly students while retaining much of teacher performance. Its effectiveness spans supervised, self-supervised, and cross-modal settings, but the choice of what to transfer (logits, features, intermediate representations, attention), how to measure discrepancy, and how to combine KD with pruning or quantization critically determines success. I argue that KD should be treated as a toolbox of complementary techniques whose components must be matched to task, teacher quality, and deployment constraints to obtain reliable and robust compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Reframing Knowledge Distillation: Beyond Strong Teachers to Regularization, Representations, and Practical Variants
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful tool for compressing deep models, but its benefits arise from multiple mechanisms beyond mere imitation of a stronger teacher. Empirical and theoretical work indicates that distillation combines regularization effects of soft targets, representational alignment, and optimization dynamics; these insights motivate a broader set of practical strategies (teacher-free or data-free distillation, feature-based objectives, contrastive and adversarial losses, ensembles, and co-training of teacher/student) to obtain compact models that generalize well. This paper argues that practitioners should select KD variants depending on data availability, deployment constraints, and the nature of the task, and that future research should prioritize understanding optimization and representation transfer rather than treating teacher capacity as the sole determinant of success.

papers_seen.author: Gibson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression methods transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or more informed teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained students. These methods are applied to reduce latency and memory, enable deployment on heterogeneous or private devices, and to retain teacher performance through tailored losses, intermediate-feature matching, multi-stage pipelines, and combinations with pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Empirical work shows KD succeeds across modalities (language, vision, multimodal, and generative models) when design choices — what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and which data to use — are matched to the task and constraints. Ongoing challenges include distilling rare-token behaviors, handling severe data heterogeneity, ensuring privacy and fairness, and automating student architecture design.

papers_seen.author: Roman
papers_seen.title: Fair Feature Distillation for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Fairness is becoming an increasingly crucial issue for computer vision, especially in the human-related decision systems. However, achieving algorithmic fairness, which makes a model produce indiscriminative outcomes against protected groups, is still an unresolved problem. In this paper, we devise a systematic approach which reduces algorithmic biases via feature distillation for visual recognition tasks, dubbed as MMD-based Fair Distillation (MFD). While the distillation technique has been widely used in general to improve the prediction accuracy, to the best of our knowledge, there has been no explicit work that also tries to improve fairness via distillation. Furthermore, We give a theoretical justification of our MFD on the effect of knowledge distillation and fairness. Throughout the extensive experiments, we show our MFD significantly mitigates the bias against specific minorities without any loss of the accuracy on both synthetic and real-world face datasets.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable ones. When paired with task-aware objectives, data strategies (including data-free synthesis), and complementary compression techniques, KD can preserve much of teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Effective use of KD requires deliberate choices about what to transfer, which data to use or synthesize, and how to align teacher and student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller student models to reduce compute, memory, and latency while preserving task performance. Across vision, speech, and language tasks, KD has been adapted into many forms—soft-target matching, intermediate representation alignment, attention and relational transfers, multi-teacher ensembles, online distillation, and task-adaptive pipelines—and combined with orthogonal compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to enable deployment in resource-constrained or privacy-sensitive settings. Empirical work shows KD often recovers most of a teacher's utility in a much smaller footprint, but success depends on teacher quality, the choice of distilled signals, data availability and domain shift, and robustness and privacy constraints. The field continues to refine objectives, layer-mapping strategies, and workflows that make distillation effective across modalities and large pretrained models in practical deployments.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a flexible, high-impact way to compress large models into smaller, efficient ones while retaining most task performance. Modern KD methods extend beyond matching final logits to include layer- and feature-level imitation, task-aware selection of distilled information, data-free or few-shot regimes, and multi-teacher or self-distillation strategies. When combined with architecture-aware compression or search, KD enables task-adaptive, privacy-conscious, and efficient deployment of deep models in real-world NLP and vision applications.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer predictive behavior and internal structure from larger, often pre-trained teacher models into smaller, efficient student models in order to reduce latency, memory, and deployment cost while retaining task performance. Methods span matching soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, attention- or relation-based feature matching, curriculum strategies for progressively harder supervision, and task- or data-aware architecture search. Practical success depends on student capacity, availability and quality of data, whether the student itself is pre-trained, and choices about what to transfer; open challenges include preserving fairness and robustness, aligning heterogeneous architectures, and operating under privacy or data-limited conditions.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Improved Feature Distillation via Projector Ensemble
papers_seen.abstract: In knowledge distillation, previous feature distillation methods mainly focus on the design of loss functions and the selection of the distilled layers, while the effect of the feature projector between the student and the teacher remains under-explored. In this paper, we first discuss a plausible mechanism of the projector with empirical evidence and then propose a new feature distillation method based on a projector ensemble for further performance improvement. We observe that the student network benefits from a projector even if the feature dimensions of the student and the teacher are the same. Training a student backbone without a projector can be considered as a multi-task learning process, namely achieving discriminative feature extraction for classification and feature matching between the student and the teacher for distillation at the same time. We hypothesize and empirically verify that without a projector, the student network tends to overfit the teacher's feature distributions despite having different architecture and weights initialization. This leads to degradation on the quality of the student's deep features that are eventually used in classification. Adding a projector, on the other hand, disentangles the two learning tasks and helps the student network to focus better on the main feature extraction task while still being able to utilize teacher features as a guidance through the projector. Motivated by the positive effect of the projector in feature distillation, we propose an ensemble of projectors to further improve the quality of student features. Experimental results on different datasets with a series of teacher-student pairs illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central approach to compress large deep models into smaller, faster, and often more deployable student models. KD techniques range from classic teacher-to-student soft-target training to recent advances including data-free distillation, multi-teacher strategies, meta-learned teachers, and compression combined with pruning or structural sparsity. In NLP applications KD is used to shrink pre-trained transformers, accelerate inference for production systems, enable non-autoregressive generation, and adapt large models to resource-constrained or heterogeneous environments. Empirical work shows KD can preserve much of teacher performance while producing models with far lower latency and storage cost, but theoretical understanding, sensitivity to data and teacher quality, and robustness under distributional shifts remain active research areas.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a broadly applicable toolkit for transferring capability from large, expensive teacher models to smaller, faster, or more privacy-friendly student models. Methods range from transferring softened output distributions to aligning intermediate representations, using synthetic or augmented data when original data are unavailable, and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). KD is used both as a deployment-oriented compression strategy and as a general training paradigm that can improve regularization, robustness, and domain adaptation. Practical success requires careful matching of distillation objectives, teacher-student alignment, and data strategies; persistent challenges include theoretical understanding of when distillation helps, preserving rare-token behavior in NLP, and avoiding artifacts introduced by synthetic data.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques transfer predictive behavior and internal structure from larger teacher models to smaller student models to reduce computation, memory, and latency while preserving performance. The literature documents a spectrum of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or channel maps, and relational signals), a variety of optimization and architectural practices (layer mapping, projectors, multi-stage training, and student-friendly teacher design), and deployment workflows for constrained settings (data-free, federated, and domain-adaptive distillation). Empirical and theoretical work highlights multiple mechanisms that make KD effective (regularization via soft targets, representation alignment, and optimization/inductive-bias transfer), while also identifying persistent challenges such as aligning heterogeneous architectures, preserving low-frequency behavior, and selecting what and when to transfer. Practical recommendations center on matching distillation signals to student capacity, using feature- or layer-aware objectives when internal alignment matters, and combining KD with complementary compression techniques for robust deployment.

papers_seen.author: Warner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression and Adaptation in NLP and Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as a central, practical technique for compressing and adapting large deep models into smaller, deployable students. KD is versatile: it transfers predictive behavior, intermediate representations, and ensemble knowledge; supports data-free or privacy-sensitive settings; and can improve robustness and calibration when combined with complementary methods. Realizing KD’s full potential requires matching the distillation recipe to deployment goals and addressing failure modes such as optimization mismatches, bias transfer, and poor handling of low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central technique for compressing large deep learning models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teachers' performance. Across vision, language, speech, and recommendation tasks, researchers combine KD with architectural compression, pre-training, privacy mechanisms, and data-free approaches to address inference cost, dataset availability, and domain-specific challenges. Empirical work shows that careful choices about what to transfer (logits, features, layers), how to train teachers and students, and how to incorporate task or data constraints strongly determine final student quality.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques have matured into a diverse set of approaches that trade off capacity, latency, and privacy to deploy high-performing deep models in constrained settings. Methods operate at different places in the training pipeline: compressing via soft-targets, transferring intermediate representations, searching or adapting compact architectures, or avoiding access to original data. Work across modalities (vision, language, graphs, generative models, and medical imaging) shows that careful choice of what to transfer (logits, relations, feature directions, layer mappings) and how to transfer it (attention, contrastive alignment, adversarial generators, or task-aware filters) determines final student performance. Practical concerns such as domain adaptation, federated and heterogeneous-device settings, and data augmentation interact strongly with distillation design choices. The literature suggests a clear pattern: representation-level and layer-aware transfers often outperform naive logits-only approaches for structured or pre-trained models, while teacher-free, data-free, and communication-efficient variants enable distillation under realistic deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: On Representation Knowledge Distillation for Graph Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a learning paradigm for boosting resource-efficient graph neural networks (GNNs) using more expressive yet cumbersome teacher models. Past work on distillation for GNNs proposed the Local Structure Preserving loss (LSP), which matches local structural relationships defined over edges across the student and teacher's node embeddings. This paper studies whether preserving the global topology of how the teacher embeds graph data can be a more effective distillation objective for GNNs, as real-world graphs often contain latent interactions and noisy edges. We propose Graph Contrastive Representation Distillation (G-CRD), which uses contrastive learning to implicitly preserve global topology by aligning the student node embeddings to those of the teacher in a shared representation space. Additionally, we introduce an expanded set of benchmarks on large-scale real-world datasets where the performance gap between teacher and student GNNs is non-negligible. Experiments across 4 datasets and 14 heterogeneous GNN architectures show that G-CRD consistently boosts the performance and robustness of lightweight GNNs, outperforming LSP (and a global structure preserving variant of LSP) as well as baselines from 2D computer vision. An analysis of the representational similarity among teacher and student embedding spaces reveals that G-CRD balances preserving local and global relationships, while structure preserving approaches are best at preserving one or the other. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practical Trends
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques aim to transfer predictive power from large teacher models into smaller, faster, or more private student models while retaining most of the original performance. Work across vision and language has expanded KD beyond simple logit matching into data-centric methods (augmentation and mixup), layer- and representation-level transfers, task-adaptive architecture search, data-free and privacy-aware distillation, and unified pipelines that combine pruning or structural compression with distillation. The field blends empirical engineering (speed/size trade-offs) with emerging theoretical analyses that help explain when and why distillation helps.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques aim to transfer predictive capacity from large, expensive models into smaller, faster models while preserving performance. Approaches vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, feature projectors), how teachers are constructed (single teacher, multi-teacher, self-teaching, or meta-learned teachers), and what resources are available (original data, public data, or no data). Practical extensions address domain-specific needs (e.g., BERT compression, low-precision deployment, privacy-preserving and federated settings) and include strategies such as progressive module replacement, multi-stage distillation, adversarially generated synthetic data, and self-supervised distillation. Empirical and theoretical work highlights both the power of soft targets as a regularizer and the importance of aligning internal representations and layer correspondences to improve student generalization.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Practical, Versatile Path to Compact and Generalizable Deep Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical suite of techniques that enable deployment of powerful deep models in resource-constrained or privacy-sensitive settings. Across modalities and tasks, KD compresses capacity while retaining much of the teacher's performance, and when combined with representation-level matching, data augmentation, curriculum strategies, meta-learning, or architecture-aware search it can also improve generalization, robustness, and cross-device inclusivity. KD is therefore not merely a model-compression trick but a broadly applicable framework for transferring structure, relational signals, and inductive biases from expensive models into efficient students for real-world use.

papers_seen.author: Wagner
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation in Natural Language Processing
papers_seen.abstract: Since deep learning became a key player in natural language processing (NLP), many deep learning models have been showing remarkable performances in a variety of NLP tasks, and in some cases, they are even outperforming humans. Such high performance can be explained by efficient knowledge representation of deep learning models. While many methods have been proposed to learn more efficient representation, knowledge distillation from pretrained deep networks suggest that we can use more information from the soft target probability to train other neural networks. In this paper, we propose a new knowledge distillation method self-knowledge distillation, based on the soft target probabilities of the training model itself, where multimode information is distilled from the word embedding space right below the softmax layer. Due to the time complexity, our method approximates the soft target probabilities. In experiments, we applied the proposed method to two different and fundamental NLP tasks: language model and neural machine translation. The experiment results show that our proposed method improves performance on the tasks.

papers_seen.author: Moran
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical family of methods for transferring predictive capacity from larger teacher models into smaller, more efficient students so models can be deployed under latency, memory, or privacy constraints. Research over the past decade has expanded simple logit-matching into a rich set of variants—feature and layer alignment, progressive module replacement, self-distillation, data-free synthesis, and privacy-aware ensembles—making KD a cornerstone of modern model-compression toolkits.

papers_seen.author: Murillo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Pragmatic Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students across modalities and tasks. KD reliably reduces inference cost and memory while preserving much of teacher performance, but it is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on design choices about what to transfer, how to handle data limitations, and how to combine distillation with complementary compression and fairness-preserving techniques. I argue that KD should be treated as a central component of a model-compression pipeline — one that is combined with architecture-aware methods, data and curriculum strategies, and explicit checks for robustness, privacy, and bias — to achieve deployable, efficient, and responsible models in practice.

papers_seen.author: Munoz
papers_seen.title: Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation in Deep Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation deals with the problem of training a smaller model (Student) from a high capacity source model (Teacher) so as to retain most of its performance. Existing approaches use either the training data or meta-data extracted from it in order to train the Student. However, accessing the dataset on which the Teacher has been trained may not always be feasible if the dataset is very large or it poses privacy or safety concerns (e.g., bio-metric or medical data). Hence, in this paper, we propose a novel data-free method to train the Student from the Teacher. Without even using any meta-data, we synthesize the Data Impressions from the complex Teacher model and utilize these as surrogates for the original training data samples to transfer its learning to Student via knowledge distillation. We, therefore, dub our method "Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation" and demonstrate that our framework results in competitive generalization performance as achieved by distillation using the actual training data samples on multiple benchmark datasets.

papers_seen.author: Montoya
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of methods for transferring behavior from large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models so they can be deployed under real-world constraints. Approaches vary in what is transferred (soft outputs, internal features, attention maps, module behavior), whether distillation is offline, online, or federated, and how it is combined with architecture search, pruning, or privacy mechanisms. Empirically, KD routinely improves compact models over training from scratch and enables deployments across on-device, distributed, and data-scarce settings; however, practical success depends on aligning distillation signals to student capacity, handling imperfect or heterogeneous teachers, and addressing data and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Mahoney
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Context-Sensitive Path to Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible technique for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact student models. When combined with feature-level objectives, architectural transformations, teacher optimization, and data strategies, KD can recover much of a teacher's performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, its success depends on task and domain specifics, teacher quality, student capacity, and data availability; therefore, practitioners should treat KD as a toolbox to be adapted—not a single recipe—to obtain reliable compression in real-world systems.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques aim to transfer information from large, expensive teacher models into smaller, faster students while preserving performance. This synthesis summarizes methodological families (soft-label distillation, representation distillation, adversarial and decision-boundary approaches, data-free and domain-adaptive strategies), theoretical insights about when and why distillation helps, and practical considerations including robustness, privacy, and architecture-aware compression. It highlights representative results and trade-offs reported across recent work, and outlines open directions for improving optimization, preserving robustness, and adapting distillation to domain and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression methods aim to transfer performance and representational properties from large, expensive models to smaller, efficient ones. Across tasks in vision, language, graph learning, and generative modeling, researchers have developed strategies that extend beyond matching final logits: layer-wise and representation matching, many-to-many layer alignment, data-free distillation, private/distilled deployment, multi-teacher and self-distillation schemes, and task-adaptive compression. These approaches trade off fidelity, privacy, and computational cost, and they have been shown to enable real-world deployment of pretrained language models and other deep systems while revealing open challenges in distribution shift, heterogeneous data, and preserving inductive biases.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Practical, Careful, and Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, widely applicable approach to compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. When applied thoughtfully, KD enables deployment under resource, latency, and privacy constraints; supports domain adaptation and vocabulary specialization; and can be combined with other compression techniques. However, its success depends on careful choices about what to transfer (logits vs. features), how to align layers and representations, how to generate or augment data for distillation, and how to mitigate propagated errors or biases from teachers.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques reduce the size, memory, and inference cost of large neural networks by transferring knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller student models. Across tasks and modalities—classification, detection, generative modeling, retrieval, and NLP—research has developed logits-based, feature-based, and task-adapted distillation strategies, multi-teacher and ensemble approaches, privacy- and communication-conscious protocols for distributed settings, and teacher-optimization/meta-learning variants. These methods trade off fidelity to teacher behavior with student capacity, expose failure modes (e.g., transfer of low-frequency lexical mistakes or overfitting of student features), and introduce remedies such as selective sample distillation, feature projectors, adversarially-informed samples, and staged or multi-teacher curricula. While KD consistently improves compact models compared to training from scratch and enables deployment on resource-constrained platforms, open issues remain in robustness, task-specific alignment, and distillation under data heterogeneity.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Methods, Theory, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses and transfers knowledge from larger, often ensemble or teacher models into smaller student models to enable efficient deployment and improved generalization under resource constraints. Techniques range from matching final soft outputs to aligning intermediate representations, leveraging self-supervision, adversarial objectives, or curriculum and sample selection strategies. Distillation has been applied across classification, generation, retrieval, speech, and structured prediction, and it also offers avenues to transfer inductive biases, improve robustness, and preserve privacy. Empirical and theoretical work has clarified when distillation helps, what kind of "dark knowledge" is useful, and how regularization-like effects of soft targets can be harnessed even without a superior teacher.

papers_seen.author: Mills
papers_seen.title: Why Knowledge Distillation Should Be the Central Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, adaptable technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of their performance. When combined with careful pre-training of compact architectures, representation-level transfer, augmentation or synthesized data, and orthogonal compression methods (pruning, quantization), KD delivers strong trade-offs between efficiency and accuracy. However, realizing those gains in practice requires attention to optimization dynamics, data availability, privacy, and known failure modes (e.g., low-frequency token degradation), and so KD should be applied as part of an integrated, responsible compression pipeline.

Methods span matching soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, attention- or relation-based feature matching, curriculum strategies for progressively harder supervision, and task- or data-aware architecture search. Practical success depends on student capacity, availability and quality of data, whether the student itself is pre-trained, and choices about what to transfer; open challenges include preserving fairness and robustness, aligning heterogeneous architectures, and operating under privacy or data-limited conditions.

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practical Trends
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques aim to transfer predictive power from large teacher models into smaller, faster, or more private student models while retaining most of the original performance. Work across vision and language has expanded KD beyond simple logit matching into data-centric methods (augmentation and mixup), layer- and representation-level transfers, task-adaptive architecture search, data-free and privacy-aware distillation, and unified pipelines that combine pruning or structural compression with distillation. The field blends empirical engineering (speed/size trade-offs) with emerging theoretical analyses that help explain when and why distillation helps.

papers_seen.author: Carr
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Cornerstone for Compressing Deep Models in NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic, versatile mechanism for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable ones in NLP and related modalities. When paired with targeted choices—what signals to transfer (logits versus features), how to align layers, teacher design, and data strategies—KD preserves much of the teacher’s capability while reducing compute, memory, and latency. However, KD is not a universal remedy: its success depends on optimization details, data availability, and careful engineering to handle distribution shift, rare behaviors, and student–teacher mismatches.

papers_seen.author: Cameron
papers_seen.title: Well-Read Students Learn Better: On the Importance of Pre-training Compact Models
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in natural language representations have been accompanied by large and expensive models that leverage vast amounts of general-domain text through self-supervised pre-training. Due to the cost of applying such models to down-stream tasks, several model compression techniques on pre-trained language representations have been proposed (Sun et al., 2019; Sanh, 2019). However, surprisingly, the simple baseline of just pre-training and fine-tuning compact models has been overlooked. In this paper, we first show that pre-training remains important in the context of smaller architectures, and fine-tuning pre-trained compact models can be competitive to more elaborate methods proposed in concurrent work. Starting with pre-trained compact models, we then explore transferring task knowledge from large fine-tuned models through standard knowledge distillation. The resulting simple, yet effective and general algorithm, Pre-trained Distillation, brings further improvements. Through extensive experiments, we more generally explore the interaction between pre-training and distillation under two variables that have been under-studied: model size and properties of unlabeled task data. One surprising observation is that they have a compound effect even when sequentially applied on the same data. To accelerate future research, we will make our 24 pre-trained miniature BERT models publicly available.
